# About

 Image 

![Image 2: Congressman Vicente Gonzalez with Congresswoman Nancy Pelosi](http://gonzalez.house.gov/sites/evo-subsites/gonzalez-evo.house.gov/files/styles/evo_featured_image/public/featured_image/IMG_0208.jpg?h=66fafea3&itok=8BGC5LTf)

Vicente Gonzalez is currently serving his fifth term in the United States Congress. He is the elected representative for the 34th District of Texas, which encompasses eastern Hidalgo County, and all of Cameron, Kenedy, Kleberg, and Willacy Counties.

Congressman Gonzalez earned his GED in 1985 before attending Del Mar College where he received an Associate's degree in Banking and Finance in 1990. He worked his way through college at Embry Riddle University where many of his classmates were active duty military personnel. He earned a Bachelor's degree in Business Aviation in 1992 and later earned a Juris Doctorate degree from Texas Wesleyan University School of Law (now Texas A&M School of Law) in 1996. In 1997, Congressman Gonzalez opened his law practice, V. Gonzalez & Associates.

Congressman Gonzalez is a member of the House Committee on Financial Services, where he sits on the Subcommittee on Capital Markets and the Subcommittee on National Security, Illicit Finance, and International Financial Institutions.He is also a member of the U.S. - Mexico Interparliamentary Group. Congressman Gonzalez is the current Communications and Outreach Co-Chair for the Blue Dog Coalition.

A lifetime resident of South Texas, Congressman Gonzalez is married to Lorena Saenz Gonzalez, a former teacher and school administrator in Edinburg and McAllen. They reside in the Rio Grande Valley.

**Mayra Nohemi Flores** (born January 1, 1986) is an American politician who represented [Texas's 34th congressional district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas's_34th_congressional_district "Texas's 34th congressional district") in the [United States House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives") from 2022 to 2023. A member of the [Republican Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)"), she was the first female [Mexican-born](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexican_Americans "Mexican Americans") member of the House.

Flores was born in [Burgos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgos_Municipality,_Tamaulipas "Burgos Municipality, Tamaulipas"), [Tamaulipas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tamaulipas "Tamaulipas"), Mexico; her family moved to the United States when she was six years old before she gained [citizenship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_nationality_law "United States nationality law") at age 14. She graduated from [San Benito High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Benito_High_School_(Texas) "San Benito High School (Texas)") and [South Texas College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Texas_College "South Texas College"). Before her congressional campaign, she worked as a [respiratory therapist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Respiratory_therapist "Respiratory therapist") and as chair of Hispanic outreach for the [Hidalgo County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hidalgo_County,_Texas "Hidalgo County, Texas") Republican Party. In June 2022, a [special election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Texas's_34th_congressional_district_special_election "2022 Texas's 34th congressional district special election") in Texas's 34th congressional district was held after [Democratic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)") Representative [Filemon Vela Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filemon_Vela_Jr. "Filemon Vela Jr.") resigned. Flores won the election, defeating three other candidates.

Flores lost her campaign for a full term in the [November 2022 midterm elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections_in_Texas#District_34 "2022 United States House of Representatives elections in Texas") to Democrat [Vicente Gonzalez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vicente_Gonzalez_(American_politician) "Vicente Gonzalez (American politician)") in the district that was redrawn that year.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-NBCews11092022-3) In 2024, Flores challenged Gonzalez again, but narrowly lost the general election. In 2026, Flores ran again, but lost the district's Republican primary.

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mayra_Flores&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Mayra Nohemi Flores was born on January 1, 1986, in [Burgos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgos_Municipality,_Tamaulipas "Burgos Municipality, Tamaulipas"), [Tamaulipas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tamaulipas "Tamaulipas"), Mexico, to migrant farmworkers. Her family moved to the U.S. when she was six years old and she gained [citizenship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_nationality_law "United States nationality law") at 14. She graduated from [San Benito High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Benito_High_School_(Texas) "San Benito High School (Texas)") in 2004.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-4)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-SANews04112022-5) Her family often moved yearly throughout Texas during her childhood because of her and her parents' work [picking cotton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cotton#Harvesting "Cotton"), which began in [Memphis, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memphis,_Texas "Memphis, Texas"), when she was 13.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-NYT-6)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-7) She graduated from [South Texas College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Texas_College "South Texas College") in 2019.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-NYT-6)

## Early political career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mayra_Flores&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early political career")]

Flores's parents supported the [Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)"), but she was drawn to the [Republican Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)") due to her [anti-abortion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_anti-abortion_movement "United States anti-abortion movement") views.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-NYT-6) She has said that she was previously a Democrat, but left the party shortly after voting for [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") in the [2008 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_United_States_presidential_election "2008 United States presidential election").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-8)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-9)

Before her congressional campaigns and shortly after graduating from college, Flores worked in the [Hidalgo County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hidalgo_County,_Texas "Hidalgo County, Texas") Republican Party as chair of Hispanic outreach.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-10)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-NYT-6) In 2022, she organized pro-[Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") caravans through the [Rio Grande Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_Rio_Grande_Valley "Lower Rio Grande Valley").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-MedinaJuly22-11) Before her election to Congress, Flores used [hashtags](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hashtag "Hashtag") associated with the [QAnon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/QAnon "QAnon") conspiracy theory on an [Instagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instagram "Instagram") post, though she has denied ever being a supporter of QAnon.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-SANews04112022-5) In tweets that she later deleted, Flores also promoted the false claim that the [2021 United States Capitol attack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_United_States_Capitol_attack "2021 United States Capitol attack") was "set up" by [antifa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antifa_(United_States) "Antifa (United States)") members among the crowd during the riot.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-MedinaJuly22-11)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-12)

## U.S. House of Representatives

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mayra_Flores&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: U.S. House of Representatives")]

### Elections

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mayra_Flores&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Elections")]

#### 2022 special

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mayra_Flores&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 2022 special")]

See also: [2022 Texas's 34th congressional district special election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Texas's_34th_congressional_district_special_election "2022 Texas's 34th congressional district special election")

Flores declared her candidacy for the [United States House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives") in [Texas's 34th congressional district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas's_34th_congressional_district "Texas's 34th congressional district") after incumbent Democratic representative [Filemon Vela Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filemon_Vela_Jr. "Filemon Vela Jr.") announced in March 2021 that he would not seek reelection in 2022.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-Vela-13)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-14) She ran her campaign appealing to [Hispanic and Latino Americans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hispanic_and_Latino_Americans "Hispanic and Latino Americans") and their disillusionment with the Democratic Party, which they have historically supported in [South Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Texas "South Texas").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-15) Following the establishment of new [congressional districts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas's_congressional_districts "Texas's congressional districts") as a part of the [2020 redistricting cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_redistricting_cycle "2020 United States redistricting cycle"), incumbent Democrat [Vicente Gonzalez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vicente_Gonzalez_(American_politician) "Vicente Gonzalez (American politician)") of the [15th district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas's_15th_congressional_district "Texas's 15th congressional district") announced his candidacy for the new 34th district.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-16) On March 1, 2022, Flores and Gonzalez won their respective partisan primaries and faced each other in the general election on November 8, 2022.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-17)

In March 2022, Vela announced his early resignation from Congress.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-18) Shortly after his announcement, Flores declared her candidacy in the special election on June 14, 2022, to fill the vacancy.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-19) Gonzalez did not run in the special election.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-20) Flores's campaign focused on her family, the economy, border security, and her upbringing as the daughter of immigrants.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-Tribune-21) During the special election, Flores reported $752,000 in contributions, while Democrat Dan Sanchez of [Harlingen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harlingen,_Texas "Harlingen, Texas") reported $46,000.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-TXTrib06142022-22) Turnout was incredibly low at only 7.3% of registered voters participating in the election.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-23) Flores defeated Sanchez with 50.91% of the vote to Sanchez's 43.37%, avoiding a runoff.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-TXTrib06142022-22) She is the first Mexican-born woman elected to serve in Congress.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-SANews04112022-5)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-TXTrib06142022-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-24)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-25)

#### 2022 general

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mayra_Flores&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 2022 general")]

See also: [2022 United States House of Representatives elections in Texas §District 34](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections_in_Texas#District_34 "2022 United States House of Representatives elections in Texas")

In her general election campaign against Democrat Vincente Gonzalez, Flores was targeted with racist and sexist comments; a blogger who had previously received funds from the Gonzalez campaign called her "Miss Frijoles", "Miss Enchiladas", and a "cotton-pickin' liar".[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-26) Gonzalez and district Democrats condemned these comments. Gonzalez also called Flores "unqualified" and claimed she could not "think or speak for herself", criticisms that were called sexist.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-Frijoles-27)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-28)

In the November 8 general election, Gonzalez defeated Flores 53% to 44%, to become the next Representative for the 34th District.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-NBCews11092022-3)

#### 2024

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mayra_Flores&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: 2024")]

Main article: [2024 United States House of Representatives elections in Texas §District 34](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections_in_Texas#District_34 "2024 United States House of Representatives elections in Texas")

On July 11, 2023, Flores announced a campaign to retake the 34th district in the 2024 election.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-TexasTribune-2024Campaign-29)

In what the _Texas Tribune_ called "a bizarre micro-scandal", in January 2024 Flores was accused by a social media user of stealing photos of food and presenting them as her own on her campaign's social media accounts. Flores initially blocked critics and changed the name of her social media account, but later said she had "no intention to mislead" and that the photos reminded her of her childhood upbringing in Mexico.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-30)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-31)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-32)

Flores prevailed in a contested primary election on March 5, 2024.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-TheTexan-2024Primary-33)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-TexasTribune-2024Campaign-29) She received millions of dollars of campaign funding from other House Republicans and increased Republican voter turnout, but lost the election against incumbent Democrat [Vicente Gonzalez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vicente_Gonzalez_(American_politician) "Vicente Gonzalez (American politician)") in the November general election by 5,137 votes, 51.3% to 48.7% .[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-TexasTribute-2024Results-34) Flores campaigned in churches in a potential violation of federal regulations.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-35)

#### 2026

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mayra_Flores&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: 2026")]

Main article: [2026 United States House of Representatives elections in Texas §District 34](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections_in_Texas#District_34 "2026 United States House of Representatives elections in Texas")

On April 15, 2025, Flores announced that she would challenge Democratic Representative [Henry Cuellar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Cuellar "Henry Cuellar") in [Texas's 28th congressional district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas's_28th_congressional_district "Texas's 28th congressional district").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-36)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-37) However, she switched her bid back to [Texas's 34th congressional district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas's_34th_congressional_district "Texas's 34th congressional district") in August 2025 after redistricting made the district more favorable for Republicans.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-38)

### Tenure

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mayra_Flores&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Tenure")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/85/Mayra_Flores_sworn_in.png/250px-Mayra_Flores_sworn_in.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mayra_Flores_sworn_in.png)

House Speaker [Nancy Pelosi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi "Nancy Pelosi")_(left)_ swears in Flores, as her husband looks on

Flores was sworn in by [Speaker of the House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speaker_of_the_United_States_House_of_Representatives "Speaker of the United States House of Representatives")[Nancy Pelosi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi "Nancy Pelosi") on June 21, 2022.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-39) Three days later, Flores spoke out about the [Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States "Supreme Court of the United States") opinion in _[Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dobbs\_v.\_Jackson\_Women's\_Health\_Organization "Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization")_ which overturned _[Roe v. Wade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roe\_v.\_Wade "Roe v. Wade")_, calling the decision a "big win" and a "dream come true".[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-40)

In June 2022, Flores voted against the [Bipartisan Safer Communities Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bipartisan_Safer_Communities_Act "Bipartisan Safer Communities Act").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-41)

In July 2022, _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_ published an article about Flores's election, calling her a "far-right Latina".[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-MedinaJuly22-11) Flores responded to the article, saying _The New York Times_ knew "nothing about me or our culture" and that "I have received only hate from the liberal media".[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-42)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-43) The article was also criticized by [Ted Cruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Cruz "Ted Cruz") and [Laura Ingraham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laura_Ingraham "Laura Ingraham"), among others.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-44)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-45)

On July 19, 2022, Flores voted against the [Respect for Marriage Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Respect_for_Marriage_Act "Respect for Marriage Act").[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-:0-46)

### Political positions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mayra_Flores&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Political positions")]

Flores supports [religious freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion "Freedom of religion"), [school choice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_choice "School choice"), and [abortion bans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abortion_law "Abortion law").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-MedinaJuly22-11) She opposes [same-sex marriage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Same-sex_marriage "Same-sex marriage").[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-:0-46) She backed former President [Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") publicly and raised doubts about the results of the 2020 election.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-47)

Flores' committee assignments included:[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-48)

*   [Committee on Homeland Security](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_Committee_on_Homeland_Security "United States House Committee on Homeland Security")
    *   [Subcommittee on Border Security, Facilitation, & Operations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subcommittee_on_Border_Security,_Facilitation,_&_Operations "Subcommittee on Border Security, Facilitation, & Operations")
    *   [Subcommittee on Transportation & Maritime Security](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subcommittee_on_Transportation_&_Maritime_Security "Subcommittee on Transportation & Maritime Security")

*   [Committee on Agriculture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_Committee_on_Agriculture "House Committee on Agriculture")

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mayra_Flores&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Flores has worked as a [respiratory therapist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Respiratory_therapist "Respiratory therapist").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-NYT-6) She was married to John Vallejo, a [U.S. Border Patrol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Border_Patrol "United States Border Patrol") agent, with whom she has four children.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-SANews04112022-5) Flores announced in June 2025 that she and Vallejo had divorced earlier in the year, due to "irreconcilable differences."[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-49)

**Mayra Nohemi Flores** (born January 1, 1986) is an American politician who represented [Texas's 34th congressional district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas's_34th_congressional_district "Texas's 34th congressional district") in the [United States House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives") from 2022 to 2023. A member of the [Republican Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)"), she was the first female [Mexican-born](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexican_Americans "Mexican Americans") member of the House.

Flores was born in [Burgos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgos_Municipality,_Tamaulipas "Burgos Municipality, Tamaulipas"), [Tamaulipas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tamaulipas "Tamaulipas"), Mexico; her family moved to the United States when she was six years old before she gained [citizenship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_nationality_law "United States nationality law") at age 14. She graduated from [San Benito High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Benito_High_School_(Texas) "San Benito High School (Texas)") and [South Texas College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Texas_College "South Texas College"). Before her congressional campaign, she worked as a [respiratory therapist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Respiratory_therapist "Respiratory therapist") and as chair of Hispanic outreach for the [Hidalgo County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hidalgo_County,_Texas "Hidalgo County, Texas") Republican Party. In June 2022, a [special election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Texas's_34th_congressional_district_special_election "2022 Texas's 34th congressional district special election") in Texas's 34th congressional district was held after [Democratic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)") Representative [Filemon Vela Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filemon_Vela_Jr. "Filemon Vela Jr.") resigned. Flores won the election, defeating three other candidates.

Flores lost her campaign for a full term in the [November 2022 midterm elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections_in_Texas#District_34 "2022 United States House of Representatives elections in Texas") to Democrat [Vicente Gonzalez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vicente_Gonzalez_(American_politician) "Vicente Gonzalez (American politician)") in the district that was redrawn that year.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-NBCews11092022-3) In 2024, Flores challenged Gonzalez again, but narrowly lost the general election. In 2026, Flores ran again, but lost the district's Republican primary.

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mayra_Flores&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Mayra Nohemi Flores was born on January 1, 1986, in [Burgos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgos_Municipality,_Tamaulipas "Burgos Municipality, Tamaulipas"), [Tamaulipas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tamaulipas "Tamaulipas"), Mexico, to migrant farmworkers. Her family moved to the U.S. when she was six years old and she gained [citizenship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_nationality_law "United States nationality law") at 14. She graduated from [San Benito High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Benito_High_School_(Texas) "San Benito High School (Texas)") in 2004.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-4)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-SANews04112022-5) Her family often moved yearly throughout Texas during her childhood because of her and her parents' work [picking cotton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cotton#Harvesting "Cotton"), which began in [Memphis, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memphis,_Texas "Memphis, Texas"), when she was 13.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-NYT-6)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-7) She graduated from [South Texas College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Texas_College "South Texas College") in 2019.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-NYT-6)

## Early political career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mayra_Flores&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early political career")]

Flores's parents supported the [Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)"), but she was drawn to the [Republican Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)") due to her [anti-abortion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_anti-abortion_movement "United States anti-abortion movement") views.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-NYT-6) She has said that she was previously a Democrat, but left the party shortly after voting for [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") in the [2008 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_United_States_presidential_election "2008 United States presidential election").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-8)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-9)

Before her congressional campaigns and shortly after graduating from college, Flores worked in the [Hidalgo County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hidalgo_County,_Texas "Hidalgo County, Texas") Republican Party as chair of Hispanic outreach.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-10)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-NYT-6) In 2022, she organized pro-[Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") caravans through the [Rio Grande Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_Rio_Grande_Valley "Lower Rio Grande Valley").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-MedinaJuly22-11) Before her election to Congress, Flores used [hashtags](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hashtag "Hashtag") associated with the [QAnon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/QAnon "QAnon") conspiracy theory on an [Instagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instagram "Instagram") post, though she has denied ever being a supporter of QAnon.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-SANews04112022-5) In tweets that she later deleted, Flores also promoted the false claim that the [2021 United States Capitol attack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_United_States_Capitol_attack "2021 United States Capitol attack") was "set up" by [antifa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antifa_(United_States) "Antifa (United States)") members among the crowd during the riot.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-MedinaJuly22-11)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-12)

## U.S. House of Representatives

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mayra_Flores&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: U.S. House of Representatives")]

### Elections

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mayra_Flores&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Elections")]

#### 2022 special

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mayra_Flores&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 2022 special")]

See also: [2022 Texas's 34th congressional district special election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Texas's_34th_congressional_district_special_election "2022 Texas's 34th congressional district special election")

Flores declared her candidacy for the [United States House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives") in [Texas's 34th congressional district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas's_34th_congressional_district "Texas's 34th congressional district") after incumbent Democratic representative [Filemon Vela Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filemon_Vela_Jr. "Filemon Vela Jr.") announced in March 2021 that he would not seek reelection in 2022.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-Vela-13)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-14) She ran her campaign appealing to [Hispanic and Latino Americans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hispanic_and_Latino_Americans "Hispanic and Latino Americans") and their disillusionment with the Democratic Party, which they have historically supported in [South Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Texas "South Texas").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-15) Following the establishment of new [congressional districts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas's_congressional_districts "Texas's congressional districts") as a part of the [2020 redistricting cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_redistricting_cycle "2020 United States redistricting cycle"), incumbent Democrat [Vicente Gonzalez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vicente_Gonzalez_(American_politician) "Vicente Gonzalez (American politician)") of the [15th district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas's_15th_congressional_district "Texas's 15th congressional district") announced his candidacy for the new 34th district.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-16) On March 1, 2022, Flores and Gonzalez won their respective partisan primaries and faced each other in the general election on November 8, 2022.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-17)

In March 2022, Vela announced his early resignation from Congress.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-18) Shortly after his announcement, Flores declared her candidacy in the special election on June 14, 2022, to fill the vacancy.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-19) Gonzalez did not run in the special election.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-20) Flores's campaign focused on her family, the economy, border security, and her upbringing as the daughter of immigrants.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-Tribune-21) During the special election, Flores reported $752,000 in contributions, while Democrat Dan Sanchez of [Harlingen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harlingen,_Texas "Harlingen, Texas") reported $46,000.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-TXTrib06142022-22) Turnout was incredibly low at only 7.3% of registered voters participating in the election.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-23) Flores defeated Sanchez with 50.91% of the vote to Sanchez's 43.37%, avoiding a runoff.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-TXTrib06142022-22) She is the first Mexican-born woman elected to serve in Congress.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-SANews04112022-5)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-TXTrib06142022-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-24)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-25)

#### 2022 general

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mayra_Flores&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 2022 general")]

See also: [2022 United States House of Representatives elections in Texas §District 34](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections_in_Texas#District_34 "2022 United States House of Representatives elections in Texas")

In her general election campaign against Democrat Vincente Gonzalez, Flores was targeted with racist and sexist comments; a blogger who had previously received funds from the Gonzalez campaign called her "Miss Frijoles", "Miss Enchiladas", and a "cotton-pickin' liar".[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-26) Gonzalez and district Democrats condemned these comments. Gonzalez also called Flores "unqualified" and claimed she could not "think or speak for herself", criticisms that were called sexist.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-Frijoles-27)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-28)

In the November 8 general election, Gonzalez defeated Flores 53% to 44%, to become the next Representative for the 34th District.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-NBCews11092022-3)

#### 2024

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mayra_Flores&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: 2024")]

Main article: [2024 United States House of Representatives elections in Texas §District 34](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections_in_Texas#District_34 "2024 United States House of Representatives elections in Texas")

On July 11, 2023, Flores announced a campaign to retake the 34th district in the 2024 election.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-TexasTribune-2024Campaign-29)

In what the _Texas Tribune_ called "a bizarre micro-scandal", in January 2024 Flores was accused by a social media user of stealing photos of food and presenting them as her own on her campaign's social media accounts. Flores initially blocked critics and changed the name of her social media account, but later said she had "no intention to mislead" and that the photos reminded her of her childhood upbringing in Mexico.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-30)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-31)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-32)

Flores prevailed in a contested primary election on March 5, 2024.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-TheTexan-2024Primary-33)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-TexasTribune-2024Campaign-29) She received millions of dollars of campaign funding from other House Republicans and increased Republican voter turnout, but lost the election against incumbent Democrat [Vicente Gonzalez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vicente_Gonzalez_(American_politician) "Vicente Gonzalez (American politician)") in the November general election by 5,137 votes, 51.3% to 48.7% .[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-TexasTribute-2024Results-34) Flores campaigned in churches in a potential violation of federal regulations.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-35)

#### 2026

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mayra_Flores&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: 2026")]

Main article: [2026 United States House of Representatives elections in Texas §District 34](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections_in_Texas#District_34 "2026 United States House of Representatives elections in Texas")

On April 15, 2025, Flores announced that she would challenge Democratic Representative [Henry Cuellar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Cuellar "Henry Cuellar") in [Texas's 28th congressional district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas's_28th_congressional_district "Texas's 28th congressional district").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-36)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-37) However, she switched her bid back to [Texas's 34th congressional district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas's_34th_congressional_district "Texas's 34th congressional district") in August 2025 after redistricting made the district more favorable for Republicans.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-38)

### Tenure

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mayra_Flores&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Tenure")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/85/Mayra_Flores_sworn_in.png/250px-Mayra_Flores_sworn_in.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mayra_Flores_sworn_in.png)

House Speaker [Nancy Pelosi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi "Nancy Pelosi")_(left)_ swears in Flores, as her husband looks on

Flores was sworn in by [Speaker of the House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speaker_of_the_United_States_House_of_Representatives "Speaker of the United States House of Representatives")[Nancy Pelosi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi "Nancy Pelosi") on June 21, 2022.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-39) Three days later, Flores spoke out about the [Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States "Supreme Court of the United States") opinion in _[Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dobbs\_v.\_Jackson\_Women's\_Health\_Organization "Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization")_ which overturned _[Roe v. Wade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roe\_v.\_Wade "Roe v. Wade")_, calling the decision a "big win" and a "dream come true".[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-40)

In June 2022, Flores voted against the [Bipartisan Safer Communities Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bipartisan_Safer_Communities_Act "Bipartisan Safer Communities Act").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-41)

In July 2022, _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_ published an article about Flores's election, calling her a "far-right Latina".[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-MedinaJuly22-11) Flores responded to the article, saying _The New York Times_ knew "nothing about me or our culture" and that "I have received only hate from the liberal media".[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-42)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-43) The article was also criticized by [Ted Cruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Cruz "Ted Cruz") and [Laura Ingraham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laura_Ingraham "Laura Ingraham"), among others.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-44)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-45)

On July 19, 2022, Flores voted against the [Respect for Marriage Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Respect_for_Marriage_Act "Respect for Marriage Act").[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-:0-46)

### Political positions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mayra_Flores&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Political positions")]

Flores supports [religious freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion "Freedom of religion"), [school choice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_choice "School choice"), and [abortion bans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abortion_law "Abortion law").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-MedinaJuly22-11) She opposes [same-sex marriage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Same-sex_marriage "Same-sex marriage").[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-:0-46) She backed former President [Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") publicly and raised doubts about the results of the 2020 election.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-47)

Flores' committee assignments included:[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-48)

*   [Committee on Homeland Security](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_Committee_on_Homeland_Security "United States House Committee on Homeland Security")
    *   [Subcommittee on Border Security, Facilitation, & Operations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subcommittee_on_Border_Security,_Facilitation,_&_Operations "Subcommittee on Border Security, Facilitation, & Operations")
    *   [Subcommittee on Transportation & Maritime Security](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subcommittee_on_Transportation_&_Maritime_Security "Subcommittee on Transportation & Maritime Security")

*   [Committee on Agriculture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_Committee_on_Agriculture "House Committee on Agriculture")

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mayra_Flores&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Flores has worked as a [respiratory therapist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Respiratory_therapist "Respiratory therapist").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-NYT-6) She was married to John Vallejo, a [U.S. Border Patrol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Border_Patrol "United States Border Patrol") agent, with whom she has four children.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-SANews04112022-5) Flores announced in June 2025 that she and Vallejo had divorced earlier in the year, due to "irreconcilable differences."[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayra_Flores#cite_note-49)

# Rep. Vicente Gonzalez

Representative for Texas’s 34 th District

pronounced VEE-sen-teh // gon-ZAH-less

 Track Him  Contact Him 

Gonzalez is the representative for [Texas](https://www.govtrack.us/congress/members/TX)’s 34 th congressional district ([view map](https://www.govtrack.us/congress/members/TX/34)) and is a Democrat. He has served since Jan. 3, 2023. Gonzalez is next up for reelection in 2026 and serves until Jan. 3, 2027. He is 59 years old.

He was previously the representative for [Texas](https://www.govtrack.us/congress/members/TX)’s 15 th congressional district as a Democrat from 2017 to 2022.

 Gonzalez is a member of [New Democrat Coalition, Congressional Hispanic Caucus, and Blue Dog Coalition](https://www.govtrack.us/congress/members/caucuses). _Caucus membership information may be incomplete or out of date._

# Former GOP Rep. Mayra Flores switches districts to challenge Rep. Vicente Gonzalez for third time

 Flores, who was going to challenge Rep. Henry Cuellar, is returning to her old district after a newly passed map improves Republicans’ chances of ousting Gonzalez.

Former GOP Rep. Mayra Flores announced on Wednesday that she is switching back to her original district to challenge Rep. [Vicente Gonzalez](https://www.texastribune.org/directory/vicente-gonzalez/), D-McAllen, in 2026.

Flores’ decision to run in the 34th Congressional District comes months after [she launched a campaign](https://www.texastribune.org/2025/04/15/texas-congressional-seat-flores-cuellar/) in the 28th District against Rep. [Henry Cuellar](https://www.texastribune.org/directory/henry-cuellar/), D-Laredo, and just days after the Texas Legislature approved a new congressional map that gives Republicans better odds to capture Gonzalez’s South Texas district.

“Texas’ 34th District has become one of the top GOP pickup opportunities in the country,” Flores [wrote on social media](https://x.com/MayraFlores4TX/status/1960701627372855637). “This race is not over, and our mission is far from complete. I have unfinished business.”

Another Republican, Army veteran Eric Flores — no relation to Mayra — [announced his candidacy](https://www.texastribune.org/2025/07/21/texas-congress-eric-flores-vicente-gonzalez-34th-district/) against Gonzalez in July.

Mayra Flores represented the 34th District in 2022 for about six months after winning the seat in a special election.

She lost her reelection to Gonzalez, who [switched districts himself](https://www.texastribune.org/2021/10/23/vicente-gonzalez-congress-redistricting-2022/) when his previous seat was drawn to favor Republicans, in November 2022. Gonzalez went on to narrowly defeat Flores for a second time in 2024 by less than 3 percentage points, even as the swing seat was carried by Republican Donald Trump.

Flores is the first Mexican-born woman to serve in Congress. She immigrated to the United States, where she is now a citizen, when she was six years old, according to her campaign website.

Flores, who was endorsed by Trump in 2024, wants parents to have control over their children’s education, according to the website. She’s also focused on securing the border and strengthening Texas’ economy.

Gonzalez [acknowledged to The Texas Tribune](https://www.texastribune.org/2025/07/21/texas-congress-eric-flores-vicente-gonzalez-34th-district/) in July that changes to district maps could hinder his reelection chances.

![Image 4](https://i0.wp.com/www.texastribune.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/20260302-Rowan-Temple-Data-LS-26-scaled.jpg?resize=2000%2C1334&ssl=1)

“The only way Republicans can beat me is by cheating and changing the district maps,” he said in the July statement.

While Trump won the 34th District by 4.5 percentage points last year, the newly approved lines turn it into one he would have carried by a more decisive 10 points.

The seat is anchored in the Rio Grande Valley’s Cameron County, covering the border cities of Brownsville and Harlingen. It was redrawn to include parts of conservative Nueces County and its biggest city, Corpus Christi, while dropping parts of McAllen and Hidalgo County.

# Former GOP Rep. Mayra Flores switches districts to challenge Rep. Vicente Gonzalez for third time

 Flores, who was going to challenge Rep. Henry Cuellar, is returning to her old district after a newly passed map improves Republicans’ chances of ousting Gonzalez.

Former GOP Rep. Mayra Flores announced on Wednesday that she is switching back to her original district to challenge Rep. [Vicente Gonzalez](https://www.texastribune.org/directory/vicente-gonzalez/), D-McAllen, in 2026.

Flores’ decision to run in the 34th Congressional District comes months after [she launched a campaign](https://www.texastribune.org/2025/04/15/texas-congressional-seat-flores-cuellar/) in the 28th District against Rep. [Henry Cuellar](https://www.texastribune.org/directory/henry-cuellar/), D-Laredo, and just days after the Texas Legislature approved a new congressional map that gives Republicans better odds to capture Gonzalez’s South Texas district.

“Texas’ 34th District has become one of the top GOP pickup opportunities in the country,” Flores [wrote on social media](https://x.com/MayraFlores4TX/status/1960701627372855637). “This race is not over, and our mission is far from complete. I have unfinished business.”

Another Republican, Army veteran Eric Flores — no relation to Mayra — [announced his candidacy](https://www.texastribune.org/2025/07/21/texas-congress-eric-flores-vicente-gonzalez-34th-district/) against Gonzalez in July.

Mayra Flores represented the 34th District in 2022 for about six months after winning the seat in a special election.

She lost her reelection to Gonzalez, who [switched districts himself](https://www.texastribune.org/2021/10/23/vicente-gonzalez-congress-redistricting-2022/) when his previous seat was drawn to favor Republicans, in November 2022. Gonzalez went on to narrowly defeat Flores for a second time in 2024 by less than 3 percentage points, even as the swing seat was carried by Republican Donald Trump.

Flores is the first Mexican-born woman to serve in Congress. She immigrated to the United States, where she is now a citizen, when she was six years old, according to her campaign website.

Flores, who was endorsed by Trump in 2024, wants parents to have control over their children’s education, according to the website. She’s also focused on securing the border and strengthening Texas’ economy.

Gonzalez [acknowledged to The Texas Tribune](https://www.texastribune.org/2025/07/21/texas-congress-eric-flores-vicente-gonzalez-34th-district/) in July that changes to district maps could hinder his reelection chances.

![Image 4](https://i0.wp.com/www.texastribune.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/20260302-Rowan-Temple-Data-LS-26-scaled.jpg?resize=2000%2C1334&ssl=1)

“The only way Republicans can beat me is by cheating and changing the district maps,” he said in the July statement.

While Trump won the 34th District by 4.5 percentage points last year, the newly approved lines turn it into one he would have carried by a more decisive 10 points.

The seat is anchored in the Rio Grande Valley’s Cameron County, covering the border cities of Brownsville and Harlingen. It was redrawn to include parts of conservative Nueces County and its biggest city, Corpus Christi, while dropping parts of McAllen and Hidalgo County.

## Redistricting

### 2025-2026

_See also: [Redistricting in Texas ahead of the 2026 elections](https://ballotpedia.org/Redistricting\_in\_Texas\_ahead\_of\_the\_2026\_elections "Redistricting in Texas ahead of the 2026 elections")_
Texas voluntarily redrew its congressional map ahead of the [2026 elections](https://ballotpedia.org/United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections,_2026 "United States House of Representatives elections, 2026"). The new map shifted five Democratic districts toward Republicans according to 2024 presidential results.[[4]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-4)

[President](https://ballotpedia.org/President "President")[Donald Trump](https://ballotpedia.org/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") (R) in July 2025 urged [Texas](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas "Texas")[Republicans](https://ballotpedia.org/Republicans "Republicans") to redraw the state's [congressional district boundaries](https://ballotpedia.org/Redistricting_in_Texas_after_the_2020_census#Enacted_congressional_district_maps "Redistricting in Texas after the 2020 census") to help retain the Republican [U.S. House](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._House "U.S. House") majority in the [2026 U.S. House elections](https://ballotpedia.org/United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections,_2026 "United States House of Representatives elections, 2026").[[5]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-call-5) Ahead of the redistricting effort, Republicans represented 25 of [Texas' 38 congressional districts](https://ballotpedia.org/United_States_congressional_delegations_from_Texas "United States congressional delegations from Texas"). [Democrats](https://ballotpedia.org/Democrats "Democrats") represented twelve, and the [18th District](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas%27_18th_Congressional_District "Texas' 18th Congressional District") seat was [vacant](https://ballotpedia.org/Filling_vacancies_in_the_U.S._House_of_Representatives "Filling vacancies in the U.S. House of Representatives") following the death of [Sylvester Turner](https://ballotpedia.org/Sylvester_Turner "Sylvester Turner") (D) in March 2025.

On July 7, 2025, the [U.S. Department of Justice](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Justice "U.S. Department of Justice") sent a letter to [Texas Gov.](https://ballotpedia.org/Governor_of_Texas "Governor of Texas")[Greg Abbott](https://ballotpedia.org/Greg_Abbott "Greg Abbott") (R) and [Texas Attorney General](https://ballotpedia.org/Attorney_General_of_Texas "Attorney General of Texas")[Ken Paxton](https://ballotpedia.org/Ken_Paxton "Ken Paxton") (R) suggesting that four of Texas' congressional districts were unconstitutional racial gerrymanders, writing, "As stated below, Congressional Districts TX-09, TX-18, TX-29 and TX-33 currently constitute unconstitutional 'coalition districts' and we urge the State of Texas to rectify these race-based considerations from these specific districts."[[6]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-letter-6)

On July 21, 2025, the [Texas Legislature](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas_State_Legislature "Texas State Legislature") began a 30-day special legislative session for redistricting. Texas Republicans released a map draft on July 30, 2025, that included five additional Republican-leaning districts.[[7]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-draftreleased-7)

In early August 2025, Democratic legislators left the state to [prevent a quorum](https://ballotpedia.org/Noteworthy_state_legislative_walkouts "Noteworthy state legislative walkouts").[[8]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-9) Texas state Rep. [James Talarico](https://ballotpedia.org/James_Talarico "James Talarico") (D) wrote on _X_, "My Democratic colleagues and I just left the state of Texas to break quorum and stop Trump’s redistricting power grab. Trump is trying to rig the midterm elections right before our eyes. But first he’ll have to come through us."[[10]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-10) On August 12, 2025, Gov. Abbott said he would continue calling special sessions to redraw the state's congressional map: "There will be no reprieve for the derelict Democrats who fled the state and abandoned their duty to the people who elected them. I will continue to call special session after special session until we get this Texas first agenda passed."[[11]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-11) The first special session concluded on August 15, 2025, before a new congressional could be passed, and a second special session began.[[12]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-session2-12)[Click here](https://ballotpedia.org/Noteworthy_state_legislative_walkouts#2025 "Noteworthy state legislative walkouts") to read more about the 2025 Democratic walkout during mid-decade redistricting in Texas.

On August 20, 2025, the [Texas House](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas_House_of_Representatives "Texas House of Representatives") approved [House Bill 4](https://legislation.ballotpedia.org/elections/bill/21260) containing a new congressional map by an 88-52 vote along party lines.[[13]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-13) On August 23, 2025, the [Texas Senate](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas_State_Senate "Texas State Senate") approved the map by an 18-11 vote along party lines.[[14]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-14)[Texas Gov.](https://ballotpedia.org/Governor_of_Texas "Governor of Texas")[Greg Abbott](https://ballotpedia.org/Greg_Abbott "Greg Abbott") (R) signed the new map into law on August 29, 2025.[[15]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-signed-15) The bill text stated the new district boundaries would take effect for the [2026 elections](https://ballotpedia.org/United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections_in_Texas,_2026 "United States House of Representatives elections in Texas, 2026").[[16]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-hb4-16)

### 2020-2021

_See also: [Redistricting in Texas after the 2020 census](https://ballotpedia.org/Redistricting\_in\_Texas\_after\_the\_2020\_census "Redistricting in Texas after the 2020 census")_
Texas enacted new congressional districts on October 25, 2021. The [Senate](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas_State_Senate "Texas State Senate") released a proposed congressional map on September 27, 2021, and approved an amended version of the proposal on October 8, 2021.[[17]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-17) On October 13, 2021, the [House](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas_House_of_Representatives "Texas House of Representatives") Redistricting Committee approved an amended version of the congressional map, and both chambers of the legislature approved a finalized version of the map on October 18, 2021. The Senate approved the proposal in an 18-13 vote, and the House approved the bill in an 84-59 vote.[[18]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-18) Gov. [Greg Abbott](https://ballotpedia.org/Greg_Abbott "Greg Abbott") (R) signed the map into law on October 25, 2021.[[19]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-19) This map took effect for Texas' 2022 congressional elections.  
  
**How does redistricting in Texas work?** In Texas, both congressional and state legislative district boundaries are drawn by the [Texas State Legislature](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas_State_Legislature "Texas State Legislature"). These lines are subject to veto by the [governor](https://ballotpedia.org/Governor_of_Texas "Governor of Texas").[[20]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-txloyola-20)

If the state legislature is unable to approve a state legislative redistricting plan, a backup commission must draw the lines (the backup commission is not involved in congressional redistricting). This backup commission, established in 1948, comprises the following members:[[20]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-txloyola-20)

1.   [Lieutenant governor](https://ballotpedia.org/Lieutenant_Governor_of_Texas "Lieutenant Governor of Texas")
2.   Speaker of the [Texas House of Representatives](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas_House_of_Representatives "Texas House of Representatives")
3.   [Attorney general](https://ballotpedia.org/Attorney_General_of_Texas "Attorney General of Texas")
4.   [State comptroller](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas_Comptroller_of_Public_Accounts "Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts")
5.   [Commissioner of the General Land Office](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas_Land_Commissioner "Texas Land Commissioner")

The [Texas Constitution](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas_Constitution "Texas Constitution") requires that state legislative districts be contiguous and "that they preserve whole counties when population mandates permit."[[20]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-txloyola-20)

## District analysis

### 2026

Heading into the 2026 elections, based on results from the 2024 and 2020 presidential elections, the _Cook Partisan Voter Index_ for this district is R+3. This meant that in those two presidential elections, this district's results were 3 percentage points more Republican than the national average. This made Texas' 34th the 211th most Republican district nationally.[[24]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-24)

### 2024

Heading into the 2024 elections, based on results from the 2020 and 2016 presidential elections, the _Cook Partisan Voter Index_ for this district was D+9. This meant that in those two presidential elections, this district's results were 9 percentage points more Democratic than the national average. This made Texas' 34th the 137th most Democratic district nationally.[[25]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-25)

_Daily Kos_ calculated what the results of the [2020 presidential election](https://ballotpedia.org/Presidential_election,_2020 "Presidential election, 2020") in this district would have been following [redistricting](https://ballotpedia.org/Redistricting "Redistricting"). [Joe Biden](https://ballotpedia.org/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden") (D) would have defeated [Donald Trump](https://ballotpedia.org/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") (R) 57.3%-41.8%.[[26]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-26)

### 2022

Heading into the 2022 elections, based on results from the 2020 and 2016 presidential elections, the _Cook Partisan Voter Index_ for this district was D+9. This meant that in those two presidential elections, this district's results were 9 percentage points more Democratic than the national average. This made Texas' 34th the 137th most Democratic district nationally.[[27]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-27)

_Daily Kos_ calculated what the results of the [2020 presidential election](https://ballotpedia.org/Presidential_election,_2020 "Presidential election, 2020") in this district would have been following [redistricting](https://ballotpedia.org/Redistricting "Redistricting"). [Joe Biden](https://ballotpedia.org/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden") (D) would have received 57.3% of the vote in this district and [Donald Trump](https://ballotpedia.org/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") (R) would have received 41.8%.[[28]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-28)

### 2018

Heading into the 2018 elections, based on results from the 2016 and 2012 presidential elections, the _Cook Partisan Voter Index_ for this district was D+10. This meant that in those two presidential elections, this district's results were 10 percentage points more Democratic than the national average. This made Texas' 34th Congressional District the 119th most Democratic nationally.[[29]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-29)

_FiveThirtyEight's_ September 2018 elasticity score for states and congressional districts measured "how sensitive it is to changes in the national political environment." This district's elasticity score was 1.11. This means that for every 1 point the national political mood moved toward a party, the district was expected to move 1.11 points toward that party.[[30]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-30)

# Texas' 34th Congressional District

From Ballotpedia

 Jump to: [navigation](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#mw-navigation), [search](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#p-search)

 Texas redrew its congressional district boundaries in August 2025. Voters will elect representatives under the new map in 2026. **[Click here](https://ballotpedia.org/Redistricting_ahead_of_the_2026_elections#States_considering_redistricting_before_the_2026_elections "Redistricting ahead of the 2026 elections") to read more about mid-decade redistricting ahead of the 2026 elections.**

Texas' 34th Congressional District

Incumbent

[Vicente Gonzalez Jr.](https://ballotpedia.org/Vicente_Gonzalez_Jr.)[![Image 3: Democratic](https://cdn.ballotpedia.org/images/d/d4/Electiondot.png)](https://ballotpedia.org/Democratic_Party "Democratic")

![Image 4](https://s3.amazonaws.com/ballotpedia-api4/files/thumbs/200/200/Vicente_Gonzalez_115th_congress_photo.jpg)

Assumed office: January 3, 2023

Texas' 34th Congressional District in the [United States House of Representatives](https://ballotpedia.org/United_States_House_of_Representatives) is represented by [Vicente Gonzalez Jr.](https://ballotpedia.org/Vicente_Gonzalez_Jr.) (D).

As of the 2020 Census, Texas representatives represented an average of 767,981 residents. After the 2010 Census, each member represented 701,901 residents.

## Redistricting

### 2025-2026

_See also: [Redistricting in Texas ahead of the 2026 elections](https://ballotpedia.org/Redistricting\_in\_Texas\_ahead\_of\_the\_2026\_elections "Redistricting in Texas ahead of the 2026 elections")_
Texas voluntarily redrew its congressional map ahead of the [2026 elections](https://ballotpedia.org/United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections,_2026 "United States House of Representatives elections, 2026"). The new map shifted five Democratic districts toward Republicans according to 2024 presidential results.[[4]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-4)

[President](https://ballotpedia.org/President "President")[Donald Trump](https://ballotpedia.org/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") (R) in July 2025 urged [Texas](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas "Texas")[Republicans](https://ballotpedia.org/Republicans "Republicans") to redraw the state's [congressional district boundaries](https://ballotpedia.org/Redistricting_in_Texas_after_the_2020_census#Enacted_congressional_district_maps "Redistricting in Texas after the 2020 census") to help retain the Republican [U.S. House](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._House "U.S. House") majority in the [2026 U.S. House elections](https://ballotpedia.org/United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections,_2026 "United States House of Representatives elections, 2026").[[5]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-call-5) Ahead of the redistricting effort, Republicans represented 25 of [Texas' 38 congressional districts](https://ballotpedia.org/United_States_congressional_delegations_from_Texas "United States congressional delegations from Texas"). [Democrats](https://ballotpedia.org/Democrats "Democrats") represented twelve, and the [18th District](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas%27_18th_Congressional_District "Texas' 18th Congressional District") seat was [vacant](https://ballotpedia.org/Filling_vacancies_in_the_U.S._House_of_Representatives "Filling vacancies in the U.S. House of Representatives") following the death of [Sylvester Turner](https://ballotpedia.org/Sylvester_Turner "Sylvester Turner") (D) in March 2025.

On July 7, 2025, the [U.S. Department of Justice](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Justice "U.S. Department of Justice") sent a letter to [Texas Gov.](https://ballotpedia.org/Governor_of_Texas "Governor of Texas")[Greg Abbott](https://ballotpedia.org/Greg_Abbott "Greg Abbott") (R) and [Texas Attorney General](https://ballotpedia.org/Attorney_General_of_Texas "Attorney General of Texas")[Ken Paxton](https://ballotpedia.org/Ken_Paxton "Ken Paxton") (R) suggesting that four of Texas' congressional districts were unconstitutional racial gerrymanders, writing, "As stated below, Congressional Districts TX-09, TX-18, TX-29 and TX-33 currently constitute unconstitutional 'coalition districts' and we urge the State of Texas to rectify these race-based considerations from these specific districts."[[6]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-letter-6)

On July 21, 2025, the [Texas Legislature](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas_State_Legislature "Texas State Legislature") began a 30-day special legislative session for redistricting. Texas Republicans released a map draft on July 30, 2025, that included five additional Republican-leaning districts.[[7]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-draftreleased-7)

In early August 2025, Democratic legislators left the state to [prevent a quorum](https://ballotpedia.org/Noteworthy_state_legislative_walkouts "Noteworthy state legislative walkouts").[[8]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-9) Texas state Rep. [James Talarico](https://ballotpedia.org/James_Talarico "James Talarico") (D) wrote on _X_, "My Democratic colleagues and I just left the state of Texas to break quorum and stop Trump’s redistricting power grab. Trump is trying to rig the midterm elections right before our eyes. But first he’ll have to come through us."[[10]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-10) On August 12, 2025, Gov. Abbott said he would continue calling special sessions to redraw the state's congressional map: "There will be no reprieve for the derelict Democrats who fled the state and abandoned their duty to the people who elected them. I will continue to call special session after special session until we get this Texas first agenda passed."[[11]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-11) The first special session concluded on August 15, 2025, before a new congressional could be passed, and a second special session began.[[12]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-session2-12)[Click here](https://ballotpedia.org/Noteworthy_state_legislative_walkouts#2025 "Noteworthy state legislative walkouts") to read more about the 2025 Democratic walkout during mid-decade redistricting in Texas.

On August 20, 2025, the [Texas House](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas_House_of_Representatives "Texas House of Representatives") approved [House Bill 4](https://legislation.ballotpedia.org/elections/bill/21260) containing a new congressional map by an 88-52 vote along party lines.[[13]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-13) On August 23, 2025, the [Texas Senate](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas_State_Senate "Texas State Senate") approved the map by an 18-11 vote along party lines.[[14]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-14)[Texas Gov.](https://ballotpedia.org/Governor_of_Texas "Governor of Texas")[Greg Abbott](https://ballotpedia.org/Greg_Abbott "Greg Abbott") (R) signed the new map into law on August 29, 2025.[[15]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-signed-15) The bill text stated the new district boundaries would take effect for the [2026 elections](https://ballotpedia.org/United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections_in_Texas,_2026 "United States House of Representatives elections in Texas, 2026").[[16]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-hb4-16)

### 2020-2021

_See also: [Redistricting in Texas after the 2020 census](https://ballotpedia.org/Redistricting\_in\_Texas\_after\_the\_2020\_census "Redistricting in Texas after the 2020 census")_
Texas enacted new congressional districts on October 25, 2021. The [Senate](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas_State_Senate "Texas State Senate") released a proposed congressional map on September 27, 2021, and approved an amended version of the proposal on October 8, 2021.[[17]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-17) On October 13, 2021, the [House](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas_House_of_Representatives "Texas House of Representatives") Redistricting Committee approved an amended version of the congressional map, and both chambers of the legislature approved a finalized version of the map on October 18, 2021. The Senate approved the proposal in an 18-13 vote, and the House approved the bill in an 84-59 vote.[[18]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-18) Gov. [Greg Abbott](https://ballotpedia.org/Greg_Abbott "Greg Abbott") (R) signed the map into law on October 25, 2021.[[19]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-19) This map took effect for Texas' 2022 congressional elections.  
  
**How does redistricting in Texas work?** In Texas, both congressional and state legislative district boundaries are drawn by the [Texas State Legislature](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas_State_Legislature "Texas State Legislature"). These lines are subject to veto by the [governor](https://ballotpedia.org/Governor_of_Texas "Governor of Texas").[[20]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-txloyola-20)

If the state legislature is unable to approve a state legislative redistricting plan, a backup commission must draw the lines (the backup commission is not involved in congressional redistricting). This backup commission, established in 1948, comprises the following members:[[20]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-txloyola-20)

1.   [Lieutenant governor](https://ballotpedia.org/Lieutenant_Governor_of_Texas "Lieutenant Governor of Texas")
2.   Speaker of the [Texas House of Representatives](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas_House_of_Representatives "Texas House of Representatives")
3.   [Attorney general](https://ballotpedia.org/Attorney_General_of_Texas "Attorney General of Texas")
4.   [State comptroller](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas_Comptroller_of_Public_Accounts "Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts")
5.   [Commissioner of the General Land Office](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas_Land_Commissioner "Texas Land Commissioner")

The [Texas Constitution](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas_Constitution "Texas Constitution") requires that state legislative districts be contiguous and "that they preserve whole counties when population mandates permit."[[20]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-txloyola-20)

## District analysis

### 2026

Heading into the 2026 elections, based on results from the 2024 and 2020 presidential elections, the _Cook Partisan Voter Index_ for this district is R+3. This meant that in those two presidential elections, this district's results were 3 percentage points more Republican than the national average. This made Texas' 34th the 211th most Republican district nationally.[[24]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-24)

### 2024

Heading into the 2024 elections, based on results from the 2020 and 2016 presidential elections, the _Cook Partisan Voter Index_ for this district was D+9. This meant that in those two presidential elections, this district's results were 9 percentage points more Democratic than the national average. This made Texas' 34th the 137th most Democratic district nationally.[[25]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-25)

_Daily Kos_ calculated what the results of the [2020 presidential election](https://ballotpedia.org/Presidential_election,_2020 "Presidential election, 2020") in this district would have been following [redistricting](https://ballotpedia.org/Redistricting "Redistricting"). [Joe Biden](https://ballotpedia.org/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden") (D) would have defeated [Donald Trump](https://ballotpedia.org/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") (R) 57.3%-41.8%.[[26]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-26)

### 2022

Heading into the 2022 elections, based on results from the 2020 and 2016 presidential elections, the _Cook Partisan Voter Index_ for this district was D+9. This meant that in those two presidential elections, this district's results were 9 percentage points more Democratic than the national average. This made Texas' 34th the 137th most Democratic district nationally.[[27]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-27)

_Daily Kos_ calculated what the results of the [2020 presidential election](https://ballotpedia.org/Presidential_election,_2020 "Presidential election, 2020") in this district would have been following [redistricting](https://ballotpedia.org/Redistricting "Redistricting"). [Joe Biden](https://ballotpedia.org/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden") (D) would have received 57.3% of the vote in this district and [Donald Trump](https://ballotpedia.org/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") (R) would have received 41.8%.[[28]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-28)

### 2018

Heading into the 2018 elections, based on results from the 2016 and 2012 presidential elections, the _Cook Partisan Voter Index_ for this district was D+10. This meant that in those two presidential elections, this district's results were 10 percentage points more Democratic than the national average. This made Texas' 34th Congressional District the 119th most Democratic nationally.[[29]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-29)

_FiveThirtyEight's_ September 2018 elasticity score for states and congressional districts measured "how sensitive it is to changes in the national political environment." This district's elasticity score was 1.11. This means that for every 1 point the national political mood moved toward a party, the district was expected to move 1.11 points toward that party.[[30]](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas'_34th_Congressional_District#cite_note-30)
