## Awards Recap

_Unforgettable_ — that’s what the 34th Annual GRAMMY Awards show at Radio City Music Hall in New York was. [**Natalie Cole**](https://www.grammy.com/artists/natalie-cole/)’s salute to the music of her legendary father Nat “King” Cole was remembered with many awards — winning Record Of The Year, Album Of The Year, Song Of The Year, Best Traditional Pop Performance, Best Instrumental Arrangement Accompanying Vocals, Best Engineered Album — Non-Classical, while her producer [**David Foster**](https://www.grammy.com/artists/david-foster/) took home the GRAMMY for Producer Of The Year (Non-Classical). Accepting the Song Of The Year GRAMMY for “Unforgettable,” veteran songwriter Irving Gordon described the experience nicely. “It’s like being caught in the middle of a miracle,” he explained. “In a youth-oriented culture — where youth is worshipped — it’s nice to have a middle-aged song do something.”

All ages were represented on the show, hosted by Whoopi Goldberg. As Johnny Mathis said to his co-presenter Dionne Warwick, “I just love the GRAMMYs. On what other list would I find my name between [**Madonna**](https://www.grammy.com/artists/madonna/) and Megadeth?”

Paul Simon got things off to an impressively rhythmic start with an opening performance of “Cool, Cool River” from his _Rhythm Of The Saints_ album. A dreadlocked Seal made a memorable live American debut performing his first smash “Crazy.” [**Michael Bolton**](https://www.grammy.com/artists/michael-bolton/) sang his hit version of“When A Man Loves A Woman” and won the GRAMMY for Best Pop Vocal Performance, Male. And Mary Chapin Carpenter added a bit of Cajun spice to the proceedings by performing “Down At The Twist And Shout” with the great rootsy band BeauSoleil. After being presented with the GRAMMY for Best Country Vocal Performance, Female, by Clint Black and the legendary Roy Rogers, Carpenter thanked the group for “injecting such magic and joy” into “Down At The Twist And Shout.”

Host Goldberg added a different sort of spice and comic relief — even making perhaps the dirtiest sounding joke in GRAMMY history about the show accountants. “I must tell you Deloitte & Touche are two things I do nightly,” she said before reporting that the accountants would be heading out on tour with Guns N’ Roses.

Not everybody was joking around. When R.E.M. won the GRAMMY for Best Pop Performance By A Duo Or Group With Vocal (“Losing My Religion”) — one of their three awards for the night — singer Michael Stipe struck a progressive political note. “We’d like to urge everybody to register and vote in the United States,” Stipe said of the 1992 presidential election looming that would eventually bring Bill Clinton into his first term in office. “We need candidates who will really address important issues — homelessness, AIDS research, economic depression and national healthcare.” He said this while wearing a hat with the words “White House Stop AIDS.”

Academy President Michael Greene spoke about the government’s America 2000 plan, the Bush Administration’s educational strategy of nationwide goals in the new millennium, pointing out, “Among all the goals, the words ‘art’ or ‘music’ are not mentioned even one time. The very idea that you can educate young people in a meaningful way without music and art is simply absurd.” Then, after recognizing Muddy Waters, John Coltrane, Jimi Hendrix and James Brown with [**Lifetime Achievement Awards**](https://www.grammy.com/awards/lifetime-awards/), Greene honored Academy Executive Vice President Christine Farnon with the [**Trustees Award**](https://www.grammy.com/awards/trustee-awards/). In paying tribute to Farnon’s 30-plus years of service, he said, “From its earliest days when The Recording Academy was little more than a dream, a letterhead and a golden statue of an antique phonograph, [The Recording Academy] was nurtured and protected by a caring, deeply dedicated professional.”

Stephen Sondheim appeared to honor one of the greatest female stars of the century. “She’s as good as they come,” Sondheim told the Radio City Music Hall audience. “Tonight she is a GRAMMY legend. Her name is [**Barbra Streisand**](https://www.grammy.com/artists/barbra-streisand/).” He went on to present her with the [**GRAMMY Legend Award**](https://www.grammy.com/awards/legends/) for “her relentless pursuit of perfection.” For her part, Streisand struck a humble note: “In all honesty, I don’t feel like a legend. I feel more like a work in progress.”

## Awards Recap

_Unforgettable_ — that’s what the 34th Annual GRAMMY Awards show at Radio City Music Hall in New York was. [**Natalie Cole**](https://www.grammy.com/artists/natalie-cole/)’s salute to the music of her legendary father Nat “King” Cole was remembered with many awards — winning Record Of The Year, Album Of The Year, Song Of The Year, Best Traditional Pop Performance, Best Instrumental Arrangement Accompanying Vocals, Best Engineered Album — Non-Classical, while her producer [**David Foster**](https://www.grammy.com/artists/david-foster/) took home the GRAMMY for Producer Of The Year (Non-Classical). Accepting the Song Of The Year GRAMMY for “Unforgettable,” veteran songwriter Irving Gordon described the experience nicely. “It’s like being caught in the middle of a miracle,” he explained. “In a youth-oriented culture — where youth is worshipped — it’s nice to have a middle-aged song do something.”

All ages were represented on the show, hosted by Whoopi Goldberg. As Johnny Mathis said to his co-presenter Dionne Warwick, “I just love the GRAMMYs. On what other list would I find my name between [**Madonna**](https://www.grammy.com/artists/madonna/) and Megadeth?”

Paul Simon got things off to an impressively rhythmic start with an opening performance of “Cool, Cool River” from his _Rhythm Of The Saints_ album. A dreadlocked Seal made a memorable live American debut performing his first smash “Crazy.” [**Michael Bolton**](https://www.grammy.com/artists/michael-bolton/) sang his hit version of“When A Man Loves A Woman” and won the GRAMMY for Best Pop Vocal Performance, Male. And Mary Chapin Carpenter added a bit of Cajun spice to the proceedings by performing “Down At The Twist And Shout” with the great rootsy band BeauSoleil. After being presented with the GRAMMY for Best Country Vocal Performance, Female, by Clint Black and the legendary Roy Rogers, Carpenter thanked the group for “injecting such magic and joy” into “Down At The Twist And Shout.”

Host Goldberg added a different sort of spice and comic relief — even making perhaps the dirtiest sounding joke in GRAMMY history about the show accountants. “I must tell you Deloitte & Touche are two things I do nightly,” she said before reporting that the accountants would be heading out on tour with Guns N’ Roses.

Not everybody was joking around. When R.E.M. won the GRAMMY for Best Pop Performance By A Duo Or Group With Vocal (“Losing My Religion”) — one of their three awards for the night — singer Michael Stipe struck a progressive political note. “We’d like to urge everybody to register and vote in the United States,” Stipe said of the 1992 presidential election looming that would eventually bring Bill Clinton into his first term in office. “We need candidates who will really address important issues — homelessness, AIDS research, economic depression and national healthcare.” He said this while wearing a hat with the words “White House Stop AIDS.”

Academy President Michael Greene spoke about the government’s America 2000 plan, the Bush Administration’s educational strategy of nationwide goals in the new millennium, pointing out, “Among all the goals, the words ‘art’ or ‘music’ are not mentioned even one time. The very idea that you can educate young people in a meaningful way without music and art is simply absurd.” Then, after recognizing Muddy Waters, John Coltrane, Jimi Hendrix and James Brown with [**Lifetime Achievement Awards**](https://www.grammy.com/awards/lifetime-awards/), Greene honored Academy Executive Vice President Christine Farnon with the [**Trustees Award**](https://www.grammy.com/awards/trustee-awards/). In paying tribute to Farnon’s 30-plus years of service, he said, “From its earliest days when The Recording Academy was little more than a dream, a letterhead and a golden statue of an antique phonograph, [The Recording Academy] was nurtured and protected by a caring, deeply dedicated professional.”

Stephen Sondheim appeared to honor one of the greatest female stars of the century. “She’s as good as they come,” Sondheim told the Radio City Music Hall audience. “Tonight she is a GRAMMY legend. Her name is [**Barbra Streisand**](https://www.grammy.com/artists/barbra-streisand/).” He went on to present her with the [**GRAMMY Legend Award**](https://www.grammy.com/awards/legends/) for “her relentless pursuit of perfection.” For her part, Streisand struck a humble note: “In all honesty, I don’t feel like a legend. I feel more like a work in progress.”

The **34th Annual Grammy Awards** were held on February 25, 1992, recognizing accomplishments by musicians from the previous year (1991). Natalie Cole won the most awards (three), including Album of the Year. Paul Simon opened the show.

Where your donation goes

 Accountability and transparency are core values at the Wikimedia Foundation. We manage funds and resources to ensure that every contribution supports our mission. We have earned the Platinum Seal of Transparency from Candid (formerly GuideStar), and Charity Navigator awarded us its highest rating. You can [read our most recent annual report](https://wikimediafoundation.org/annualreports/current/) for more information about our financial health. 

45% Investment in Technology 
Nearly half of our budget goes toward supporting the technology that powers Wikipedia and other Wikimedia projects. We are constantly working to enhance the user experience for both contributors and readers, improve site security, and ensure reliable access to our websites globally. This infrastructure and product support sustain one of the top ten most visited websites in the world, all at a fraction of the cost of popular for-profit websites.

32% Support for Volunteers 
The global reach of Wikimedia projects is made possible by the hard work of volunteers from across the globe. We provide grants, legal support, and other resources to help build vibrant volunteer communities. Additionally, we promote community engagement through outreach initiatives and advocate for the growth and protection of free knowledge.

12% Allocation to Fundraising Efforts 
Donor support is crucial to sustaining Wikipedia and our other free knowledge endeavors. Our team is committed to efficient and effective fundraising throughout the year, ensuring that every contribution helps advance our mission.

11% General and Administrative Expenses 
Operational costs are essential for the smooth management and governance of the Wikimedia Foundation. These expenses help us recruit top talent and support staff around the world, empowering them to carry out the mission of the Wikimedia Foundation.

The **34th Annual Grammy Awards** were held on February 25, 1992,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/34th_Annual_Grammy_Awards#cite_note-1) recognizing accomplishments by musicians from the previous year (1991). [Natalie Cole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natalie_Cole "Natalie Cole") won the most awards (three), including [Album of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Album_of_the_Year "Grammy Award for Album of the Year"), which made her the first black woman to win the award.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/34th_Annual_Grammy_Awards#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/34th_Annual_Grammy_Awards#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/34th_Annual_Grammy_Awards#cite_note-4)

The **34th Annual Grammy Awards** were held on February 25, 1992,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/34th_Annual_Grammy_Awards#cite_note-1) recognizing accomplishments by musicians from the previous year (1991). [Natalie Cole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natalie_Cole "Natalie Cole") won the most awards (three), including [Album of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Album_of_the_Year "Grammy Award for Album of the Year"), which made her the first black woman to win the award.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/34th_Annual_Grammy_Awards#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/34th_Annual_Grammy_Awards#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/34th_Annual_Grammy_Awards#cite_note-4)

## Additional Notes

**Leadership/Ideology:** The leadership and ideology scores are not displayed for Members of Congress who introduced fewer than 10 bills, or, for ideology, for Members of Congress that have a low leadership score, as there is usually not enough data in these cases to compute reliable leadership and ideology statistics.

**Missing Bills:** We exclude bills from some statistics where the sponsor’s original intent is not in the final bill because the bill’s text was replaced in whole with unrelated provisions (i.e. it became a vehicle for passage of unrelated provisions).

**Ranking Members (RkMembs):** The chair of a committee is always selected from the political party that holds the most seats in the chamber, called the “majority party”. The “ranking member” (sometimes “RkMembs”) is the title given to the senior-most member of the committee _not_ in the majority party.

**Freshmen/Sophomores:** Freshmen and sophomores are Members of Congress whose first term (in the same chamber at the end of the 115th Congress) was the 115 th Congress (freshmen) or 114 th (sophomores). Members of Congress who took office within the last few months of a Congress are considered freshmen in the next Congress as well.

**Filemón Bartolomé Vela Jr.** ([/ˈ f ɪ l ə ˌ m ɒ n ˈ v ɛ l ə/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")[_FILL-ə-monn VELL-ə_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key"); born February 13, 1963)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filemon_Vela_Jr.#cite_note-1) is an American lobbyist, lawyer, and politician who served as the [U.S. representative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives") for [Texas's 34th congressional district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas's_34th_congressional_district "Texas's 34th congressional district") from 2013 until his resignation in 2022. He is a member of the [Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)"). Vela was also vice chair of the [Democratic National Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_National_Committee "Democratic National Committee") from January 21, 2021 to March 31, 2022, having been nominated by President [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filemon_Vela_Jr.#cite_note-2) In March 2022, Vela resigned in the middle of his term to work at [Akin Gump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akin_Gump_Strauss_Hauer_&_Feld "Akin Gump Strauss Hauer & Feld").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filemon_Vela_Jr.#cite_note-resign-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filemon_Vela_Jr.#cite_note-steps_down-4)

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Filemon_Vela_Jr.&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Vela was born in [Harlingen, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harlingen,_Texas "Harlingen, Texas"), and raised in nearby [Brownsville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brownsville,_Texas "Brownsville, Texas"). His father, [Filemon Vela Sr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filemon_Vela_Sr. "Filemon Vela Sr."), was a long-serving United States federal judge. The Reynaldo G. Garza–Filemon B. Vela United States Courthouse in Brownsville is named in Judge Vela's honor. His mother, [Blanca Sanchez Vela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blanca_Vela "Blanca Vela"), served as Brownsville's first female mayor from 1999 to 2003.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filemon_Vela_Jr.#cite_note-vela.house.gov-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filemon_Vela_Jr.#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filemon_Vela_Jr.#cite_note-7)

Filemon attended [Saint Joseph Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Joseph_Academy_(Brownsville,_Texas) "Saint Joseph Academy (Brownsville, Texas)") in Brownsville, and earned his [Bachelor of Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Arts "Bachelor of Arts") from [Georgetown University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgetown_University "Georgetown University") in 1985. During his time at Georgetown, he served as an intern at the [Federal Judicial Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Judicial_Center "Federal Judicial Center"), the research and education agency of the federal judicial system. He also served as an intern in [Solomon P. Ortiz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solomon_P._Ortiz "Solomon P. Ortiz")'s office in Washington, D.C. Vela earned his [Juris Doctor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juris_Doctor "Juris Doctor") from the [University of Texas at Austin School of Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_School_of_Law "University of Texas School of Law") in 1987.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filemon_Vela_Jr.#cite_note-vela.house.gov-5)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Filemon_Vela_Jr.&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

In _[Edinburg School District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edinburg\_Consolidated\_Independent\_School\_District "Edinburg Consolidated Independent School District") v. Landmark_, Vela represented [Edinburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edinburg,_Texas "Edinburg, Texas") to fight for more funding. In _Pharr-San Juan-Alamo Independent School District v. Landmark_, he represented the district in fighting contractors accused of building a poorly constructed school facility.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filemon_Vela_Jr.#cite_note-8)[_[better source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Questionable\_sources "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_]

## U.S. House of Representatives

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Filemon_Vela_Jr.&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: U.S. House of Representatives")]

### Elections

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Filemon_Vela_Jr.&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Elections")]

#### 2012

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Filemon_Vela_Jr.&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 2012")]

Main article: [2012 United States House of Representatives elections in Texas §District 34](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections_in_Texas#District_34 "2012 United States House of Representatives elections in Texas")

Vela ran in the newly created [34th congressional district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas's_34th_congressional_district "Texas's 34th congressional district") as a Democrat. In the May 29 primary, he ranked first in an eight-candidate field with 40% of the vote.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filemon_Vela_Jr.#cite_note-9) In the July 31 runoff, Vela defeated Denise Saenz Blanchard, 67% to 33%.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filemon_Vela_Jr.#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filemon_Vela_Jr.#cite_note-11)

In the general election, Vela defeated Republican Jessica Bradshaw, 62% to 36%.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filemon_Vela_Jr.#cite_note-12)

### Tenure

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Filemon_Vela_Jr.&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Tenure")]

In July 2013, Vela quit the [Congressional Hispanic Caucus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_Hispanic_Caucus "Congressional Hispanic Caucus") because of his opposition to the [Hoeven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hoeven "John Hoeven")-[Corker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Corker "Bob Corker") Amendment that tied border security to a [pathway to citizenship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amnesty "Amnesty"). He said "erecting more border fence drives a wedge between border communities which are culturally united".[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filemon_Vela_Jr.#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filemon_Vela_Jr.#cite_note-14)

On March 22, 2021, Vela announced that he would not seek reelection in the [2022 United States House of Representatives elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections "2022 United States House of Representatives elections").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filemon_Vela_Jr.#cite_note-15)

In August 2021, Vela joined a group of conservative Democrats, dubbed "The Unbreakable Nine", who threatened to derail the [Biden administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Joe_Biden#Administration "Presidency of Joe Biden")'s $3.5 trillion budget reconciliation package meant to tackle the nation's infrastructure.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filemon_Vela_Jr.#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filemon_Vela_Jr.#cite_note-17)

On March 24, 2022, Vela confirmed that he would resign early from Congress to take a job at [Akin Gump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akin_Gump "Akin Gump"), a lobbying and law firm.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filemon_Vela_Jr.#cite_note-resign-3) His resignation officially went into effect before midnight on March 31.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filemon_Vela_Jr.#cite_note-steps_down-4)

**Filemón Bartolomé Vela Jr.** ([/ˈ f ɪ l ə ˌ m ɒ n ˈ v ɛ l ə/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")[_FILL-ə-monn VELL-ə_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key"); born February 13, 1963)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filemon_Vela_Jr.#cite_note-1) is an American lobbyist, lawyer, and politician who served as the [U.S. representative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives") for [Texas's 34th congressional district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas's_34th_congressional_district "Texas's 34th congressional district") from 2013 until his resignation in 2022. He is a member of the [Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)"). Vela was also vice chair of the [Democratic National Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_National_Committee "Democratic National Committee") from January 21, 2021 to March 31, 2022, having been nominated by President [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filemon_Vela_Jr.#cite_note-2) In March 2022, Vela resigned in the middle of his term to work at [Akin Gump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akin_Gump_Strauss_Hauer_&_Feld "Akin Gump Strauss Hauer & Feld").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filemon_Vela_Jr.#cite_note-resign-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filemon_Vela_Jr.#cite_note-steps_down-4)

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Filemon_Vela_Jr.&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Vela was born in [Harlingen, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harlingen,_Texas "Harlingen, Texas"), and raised in nearby [Brownsville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brownsville,_Texas "Brownsville, Texas"). His father, [Filemon Vela Sr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filemon_Vela_Sr. "Filemon Vela Sr."), was a long-serving United States federal judge. The Reynaldo G. Garza–Filemon B. Vela United States Courthouse in Brownsville is named in Judge Vela's honor. His mother, [Blanca Sanchez Vela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blanca_Vela "Blanca Vela"), served as Brownsville's first female mayor from 1999 to 2003.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filemon_Vela_Jr.#cite_note-vela.house.gov-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filemon_Vela_Jr.#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filemon_Vela_Jr.#cite_note-7)

Filemon attended [Saint Joseph Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Joseph_Academy_(Brownsville,_Texas) "Saint Joseph Academy (Brownsville, Texas)") in Brownsville, and earned his [Bachelor of Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Arts "Bachelor of Arts") from [Georgetown University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgetown_University "Georgetown University") in 1985. During his time at Georgetown, he served as an intern at the [Federal Judicial Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Judicial_Center "Federal Judicial Center"), the research and education agency of the federal judicial system. He also served as an intern in [Solomon P. Ortiz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solomon_P._Ortiz "Solomon P. Ortiz")'s office in Washington, D.C. Vela earned his [Juris Doctor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juris_Doctor "Juris Doctor") from the [University of Texas at Austin School of Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_School_of_Law "University of Texas School of Law") in 1987.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filemon_Vela_Jr.#cite_note-vela.house.gov-5)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Filemon_Vela_Jr.&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

In _[Edinburg School District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edinburg\_Consolidated\_Independent\_School\_District "Edinburg Consolidated Independent School District") v. Landmark_, Vela represented [Edinburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edinburg,_Texas "Edinburg, Texas") to fight for more funding. In _Pharr-San Juan-Alamo Independent School District v. ## U.S. House of Representatives

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Filemon_Vela_Jr.&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: U.S. House of Representatives")]

### Elections

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Filemon_Vela_Jr.&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Elections")]

#### 2012

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Filemon_Vela_Jr.&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 2012")]

Main article: [2012 United States House of Representatives elections in Texas §District 34](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections_in_Texas#District_34 "2012 United States House of Representatives elections in Texas")

Vela ran in the newly created [34th congressional district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas's_34th_congressional_district "Texas's 34th congressional district") as a Democrat. In the May 29 primary, he ranked first in an eight-candidate field with 40% of the vote.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filemon_Vela_Jr.#cite_note-9) In the July 31 runoff, Vela defeated Denise Saenz Blanchard, 67% to 33%.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filemon_Vela_Jr.#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filemon_Vela_Jr.#cite_note-11)

In the general election, Vela defeated Republican Jessica Bradshaw, 62% to 36%.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filemon_Vela_Jr.#cite_note-12)

### Tenure

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Filemon_Vela_Jr.&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Tenure")]

In July 2013, Vela quit the [Congressional Hispanic Caucus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_Hispanic_Caucus "Congressional Hispanic Caucus") because of his opposition to the [Hoeven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hoeven "John Hoeven")-[Corker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Corker "Bob Corker") Amendment that tied border security to a [pathway to citizenship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amnesty "Amnesty"). He said "erecting more border fence drives a wedge between border communities which are culturally united".[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filemon_Vela_Jr.#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filemon_Vela_Jr.#cite_note-14)

On March 22, 2021, Vela announced that he would not seek reelection in the [2022 United States House of Representatives elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections "2022 United States House of Representatives elections").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filemon_Vela_Jr.#cite_note-15)

In August 2021, Vela joined a group of conservative Democrats, dubbed "The Unbreakable Nine", who threatened to derail the [Biden administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Joe_Biden#Administration "Presidency of Joe Biden")'s $3.5 trillion budget reconciliation package meant to tackle the nation's infrastructure.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filemon_Vela_Jr.#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filemon_Vela_Jr.#cite_note-17)

On March 24, 2022, Vela confirmed that he would resign early from Congress to take a job at [Akin Gump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akin_Gump "Akin Gump"), a lobbying and law firm.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filemon_Vela_Jr.#cite_note-resign-3) His resignation officially went into effect before midnight on March 31.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filemon_Vela_Jr.#cite_note-steps_down-4)

# Rep. Filemon Vela

## U.S. Representative for Texas' 34th Congressional District

![Image 2: Rep. Filemon Vela](https://lulac.org/gala21/vela2_360x360.jpg)

Congressman Filemon Vela represents the 34th Congressional District of Texas, which is anchored in Cameron County in the southernmost tip of Texas, and runs nearly 300 miles north to Gonzales County. The 34th District includes Brownsville, its largest city, as well as the King Ranch, Kingsville Naval Air Station, and the historic Texas town of Goliad. Born in Harlingen, Texas, and raised in Brownsville, Congressman Vela’s roots run deep in South Texas. His ancestors purchased land from the McAllen family to establish the Laguna Seca Ranch where the first citrus orchard in Hidalgo County was planted. President Jimmy Carter appointed Congressman Vela’s father, Filemon Vela Sr., as one of the first Hispanic federal judges, where he presided over the Southern District of Texas. Congressman Vela’s mother, Blanca Sanchez Vela, served as the first, and to this day the only, female mayor of Brownsville.   
  
 Vela attended Saint Joseph Academy in Brownsville, Texas. After graduating from Georgetown University in Washington, D.C., he attended the University of Texas School of Law. His interest in public service grew from his work helping individuals seek justice in state and federal courts as an attorney for more than 20 years in South Texas.   
  
 Congressman Vela is a member of the House Agriculture Committee, where he serves as the Chairman of the General Farm Commodities and Risk Management Subcommittee. Vela joined the panel in 2013 at the beginning of his first Congressional term and served as the Vice-Ranking Member of the full committee during the 115th Congress. He was the only Texas Democrat appointed by the House of Representatives’ Leadership to serve as a negotiator on the Conference Committee which drafted the 2014 Farm Bill, and was closely involved in its reauthorization in 2018. The Farm Bill is a comprehensive law which sets agriculture policy and funding for nutrition programs, including food stamps, for the next five years. Additionally, Congressman Vela holds seats on the Subcommittee on Livestock and Foreign Agriculture and the Subcommittee on Commodity Exchanges, Energy, and Credit.   
  
 Congressman Vela also sits on the House Armed Services Committee, where he has fought to ensure that U.S. servicemembers are prepared to respond to a range of military operations. He is committed to ensuring that servicemembers and their families have access to housing, healthcare and basic living necessities to sustain them through the challenges of military service. Congressman Vela is a member of the Subcommittee on Seapower and Projection Forces and the Subcommittee on Tactical Air and Land Forces.   
  
 In Congress, Vela has been a strong advocate for immigrant rights, education programs—including Head Start and Pell Grants for college students—and community health centers. He is vehemently opposed to the construction of a border wall and is focused on bringing peace and security to our neighbors in Matamoros and Reynosa. He is also working to bring jobs and economic development to South Texas through many efforts, including transforming the Port of Brownsville into a competitive deep water port.   
  
 Congressman Vela is married to Rose Vela, a former Justice on the Texas Court of Appeals, and they reside in Brownsville, Texas.

# Rep. Filemon Vela

## U.S. Representative for Texas' 34th Congressional District

![Image 2: Rep. Filemon Vela](https://lulac.org/gala21/vela2_360x360.jpg)

Congressman Filemon Vela represents the 34th Congressional District of Texas, which is anchored in Cameron County in the southernmost tip of Texas, and runs nearly 300 miles north to Gonzales County. The 34th District includes Brownsville, its largest city, as well as the King Ranch, Kingsville Naval Air Station, and the historic Texas town of Goliad. Born in Harlingen, Texas, and raised in Brownsville, Congressman Vela’s roots run deep in South Texas. His ancestors purchased land from the McAllen family to establish the Laguna Seca Ranch where the first citrus orchard in Hidalgo County was planted. President Jimmy Carter appointed Congressman Vela’s father, Filemon Vela Sr., as one of the first Hispanic federal judges, where he presided over the Southern District of Texas. Congressman Vela’s mother, Blanca Sanchez Vela, served as the first, and to this day the only, female mayor of Brownsville.   
  
 Vela attended Saint Joseph Academy in Brownsville, Texas. After graduating from Georgetown University in Washington, D.C., he attended the University of Texas School of Law. His interest in public service grew from his work helping individuals seek justice in state and federal courts as an attorney for more than 20 years in South Texas.   
  
 Congressman Vela is a member of the House Agriculture Committee, where he serves as the Chairman of the General Farm Commodities and Risk Management Subcommittee. Vela joined the panel in 2013 at the beginning of his first Congressional term and served as the Vice-Ranking Member of the full committee during the 115th Congress. He was the only Texas Democrat appointed by the House of Representatives’ Leadership to serve as a negotiator on the Conference Committee which drafted the 2014 Farm Bill, and was closely involved in its reauthorization in 2018. The Farm Bill is a comprehensive law which sets agriculture policy and funding for nutrition programs, including food stamps, for the next five years. Additionally, Congressman Vela holds seats on the Subcommittee on Livestock and Foreign Agriculture and the Subcommittee on Commodity Exchanges, Energy, and Credit.   
  
 Congressman Vela also sits on the House Armed Services Committee, where he has fought to ensure that U.S. servicemembers are prepared to respond to a range of military operations. He is committed to ensuring that servicemembers and their families have access to housing, healthcare and basic living necessities to sustain them through the challenges of military service. Congressman Vela is a member of the Subcommittee on Seapower and Projection Forces and the Subcommittee on Tactical Air and Land Forces.   
  
 In Congress, Vela has been a strong advocate for immigrant rights, education programs—including Head Start and Pell Grants for college students—and community health centers. He is vehemently opposed to the construction of a border wall and is focused on bringing peace and security to our neighbors in Matamoros and Reynosa. He is also working to bring jobs and economic development to South Texas through many efforts, including transforming the Port of Brownsville into a competitive deep water port.   
  
 Congressman Vela is married to Rose Vela, a former Justice on the Texas Court of Appeals, and they reside in Brownsville, Texas.

**Filemon Vela** ([Democratic Party](https://ballotpedia.org/Democratic_Party)) was a member of the [U.S. House](https://ballotpedia.org/United_States_House_of_Representatives), representing Texas' 34th Congressional District. He assumed office on January 3, 2013. He left office on April 1, 2022.

Vela ([Democratic Party](https://ballotpedia.org/Democratic_Party)) ran for re-election to the [U.S. House](https://ballotpedia.org/United_States_House_of_Representatives) to represent Texas' 34th Congressional District. He won in the general election on [November 3, 2020](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas%27_34th_Congressional_District_election,_2020).

Vela resigned on April 1, 2022 to accept a position at Akin Gump Strauss Hauer & Feld, a lobbying firm in Washington D.C.[[1]](https://ballotpedia.org/Filemon_Vela_(Texas_U.S._representative)#cite_note-1)

Vela is a member of the House Committee on Homeland Security and the House Committee on Agriculture. He is also co-chair of the Congressional Border Caucus.[[2]](https://ballotpedia.org/Filemon_Vela_(Texas_U.S._representative)#cite_note-2)

Before being elected to Congress, Vela worked as a lawyer.

On March 22, 2021, Vela announced he [would not seek re-election](https://ballotpedia.org/List_of_U.S._Congress_incumbents_who_are_not_running_for_re-election_in_2022 "List of U.S. Congress incumbents who are not running for re-election in 2022") in 2022.[[3]](https://ballotpedia.org/Filemon_Vela_(Texas_U.S._representative)#cite_note-3)

## Biography

Vela was born in Harlingen, Texas. He graduated with a bachelor's degree from Georgetown University and his law degree from University of Texas. He has worked as an attorney since his graduation. He once considered running for Congress in the 1980s but his clients kept his focus until he decided to run in 2011.[[4]](https://ballotpedia.org/Filemon_Vela_(Texas_U.S._representative)#cite_note-nj-4)

## Career

Below is an abbreviated outline of Vela's academic, professional, and political career:[[5]](https://ballotpedia.org/Filemon_Vela_(Texas_U.S._representative)#cite_note-5)

*   2013-2022: U.S. Representative from Texas' 34th Congressional District
*   1988-2012: Practicing lawyer
*   1987: Graduated from the University of Texas, Austin, with a J.D.
*   1985: Graduated from Georgetown University with a B.A.

### Key votes: 117th Congress, 2021-2023

The [117th United States Congress](https://ballotpedia.org/117th_United_States_Congress "117th United States Congress") began on January 3, 2021 and ended on January 3, 2023. At the start of the session, Democrats held the majority in the [U.S. House of Representatives](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._House_of_Representatives "U.S. House of Representatives") (222-213), and the [U.S. Senate](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Senate "U.S. Senate") had a 50-50 makeup. Democrats assumed control of the Senate on January 20, 2021, when President [Joe Biden](https://ballotpedia.org/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden") (D) and Vice President [Kamala Harris](https://ballotpedia.org/Kamala_Harris "Kamala Harris") (D), who acted as a tie-breaking vote in the chamber, assumed office. Trump vetoed the bill due to disagreement with provisions related to Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, the renaming of certain military installations, limits on emergency military construction fund usage, and limits on troop withdrawals. Comparatively, the [113th Congress](https://ballotpedia.org/113th_Congress "113th Congress") had 7.0 percent of introduced bills enacted into law in the second session.[[81]](https://ballotpedia.org/Filemon_Vela_(Texas_U.S._representative)#cite_note-81)[[82]](https://ballotpedia.org/Filemon_Vela_(Texas_U.S._representative)#cite_note-82) For more information pertaining to Vela's voting record in the 114th Congress, please see the below sections.[[83]](https://ballotpedia.org/Filemon_Vela_(Texas_U.S._representative)#cite_note-83) #### Economic and fiscal ##### Trade Act of 2015 _See also: [The Trans-Pacific Partnership trade deal, 2015](https://ballotpedia.org/The\_Trans-Pacific\_Partnership\_trade\_deal,\_2015 "The Trans-Pacific Partnership trade deal, 2015")_ **Trade adjustment assistance** [![Image 126: Nay3.png](https://cdn.ballotpedia.org/images/thumb/e/ea/Nay3.png/55px-Nay3.png)](https://ballotpedia.org/Portal:Legislative_Branch "Portal:Legislative Branch") On June 12, 2015, the [House](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._House_of_Representatives "U.S. House of Representatives") rejected the [trade adjustment assistance (TAA)](https://ballotpedia.org/Trade_adjustment_assistance "Trade adjustment assistance") measure in [HR 1314—the Trade Act of 2015](https://www.congress.gov/bill/114th-congress/house-bill/1314)—by a vote of 126-302. [Trade adjustment assistance (TAA)](https://ballotpedia.org/Trade_adjustment_assistance "Trade adjustment assistance") is a federal program providing American workers displaced by foreign trade agreements with job training and services. The measure was packaged with [trade promotion authority (TPA)](https://ballotpedia.org/Trade_promotion_authority_(TPA) "Trade promotion authority (TPA)"), also known as fast-track authority. TPA is a legislative procedure that allows Congress to define "U.S. negotiating objectives and spells out a detailed oversight and consultation process for during trade negotiations. Under TPA, Congress retains the authority to review and decide whether any proposed U.S. trade agreement will be implemented," according to the Office of the United States Trade Representative. Vela was one of 144 Democrats to vote against the bill.[[84]](https://ballotpedia.org/Filemon_Vela_(Texas_U.S._representative)#cite_note-84)[[85]](https://ballotpedia.org/Filemon_Vela_(Texas_U.S._representative)#cite_note-85) **Trade promotion authority** [![Image 127: Nay3.png](https://cdn.ballotpedia.org/images/thumb/e/ea/Nay3.png/55px-Nay3.png)](https://ballotpedia.org/Portal:Legislative_Branch "Portal:Legislative Branch") On June 12, 2015, the [House](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._House_of_Representatives "U.S. House of Representatives") passed the [trade promotion authority (TPA)](https://ballotpedia.org/Trade_promotion_authority_(TPA) "Trade promotion authority (TPA)") measure in [HR 1314—the Trade Act of 2015](https://www.congress.gov/bill/114th-congress/house-bill/1314) —by a vote of 219-211. TPA gives the [president](https://ballotpedia.org/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") fast-track authority to negotiate trade agreements sent to [Congress](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Congress "U.S. Congress") without the opportunity for amendment or filibuster. Although the House approved TPA, it was a largely symbolic vote given the measure was part of a package trade bill including [trade adjustment assistance (TAA)](https://ballotpedia.org/Trade_adjustment_assistance "Trade adjustment assistance"), which was rejected earlier the same day. Vela was one of 157 [Democrats](https://ballotpedia.org/Democrats "Democrats") to vote against the measure.[[86]](https://ballotpedia.org/Filemon_Vela_(Texas_U.S._representative)#cite_note-86)[[87]](https://ballotpedia.org/Filemon_Vela_(Texas_U.S._representative)#cite_note-87) **Trade promotion authority second vote** [![Image 128: Nay3.png](https://cdn.ballotpedia.org/images/thumb/e/ea/Nay3.png/55px-Nay3.png)](https://ballotpedia.org/Portal:Legislative_Branch "Portal:Legislative Branch") After the [trade adjustment assistance (TAA)](https://ballotpedia.org/Trade_adjustment_assistance "Trade adjustment assistance") and [trade promotion authority (TPA)](https://ballotpedia.org/Trade_promotion_authority_(TPA) "Trade promotion authority (TPA)") did not pass the [House](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._House_of_Representatives "U.S. House of Representatives") together on June 12, 2015, representatives voted to authorize TPA alone as an amendment to [HR 2146—the Defending Public Safety Employees' Retirement Act](https://www.congress.gov/bill/114th-congress/house-bill/2146/text/eah)—on June 18, 2015. The amendment passed by a vote of 218-208, with all voting members of the House maintaining his or her original position on TPA except for [Ted Yoho](https://ballotpedia.org/Ted_Yoho "Ted Yoho") (R-Fla.). Vela was one of 158 [Democrats](https://ballotpedia.org/Democrats "Democrats") to vote against the amendment.[[88]](https://ballotpedia.org/Filemon_Vela_(Texas_U.S._representative)#cite_note-88)[[89]](https://ballotpedia.org/Filemon_Vela_(Texas_U.S._representative)#cite_note-89) **Trade adjustment assistance second vote** [![Image 129: Yea3.png](https://cdn.ballotpedia.org/images/thumb/c/cd/Yea3.png/50px-Yea3.png)](https://ballotpedia.org/Portal:Legislative_Branch "Portal:Legislative Branch") The [House](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._House_of_Representatives "U.S. House of Representatives") passed [HR 1295—the Trade Preferences Extension Act of 2015](https://www.congress.gov/bill/114th-congress/house-bill/1295)—on June 25, 2015, by a vote of 286-138. The [Senate](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Senate "U.S. Senate") packaged [trade adjustment assistance (TAA)](https://ballotpedia.org/Trade_adjustment_assistance "Trade adjustment assistance") in this bill after the House rejected the TAA measure in [HR 1314—the Trade Act of 2015](https://www.congress.gov/bill/114th-congress/house-bill/1314/text). Along with [trade promotion authority (TPA)](https://ballotpedia.org/Trade_promotion_authority_(TPA) "Trade promotion authority (TPA)"), which [Congress](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Congress "U.S. Congress") passed as part of [HR 2146—the Defending Public Safety Employees' Retirement Act](https://www.congress.gov/bill/114th-congress/house-bill/2146)—TAA became law on June 29, 2015. Vela was one of 175 [Democrats](https://ballotpedia.org/Democrats "Democrats") to vote in favor of HR 1295.[[90]](https://ballotpedia.org/Filemon_Vela_(Texas_U.S._representative)#cite_note-90)[[91]](https://ballotpedia.org/Filemon_Vela_(Texas_U.S._representative)#cite_note-91) ##### Defense spending authorization [![Image 130: Nay3.png](https://cdn.ballotpedia.org/images/thumb/e/ea/Nay3.png/55px-Nay3.png)](https://ballotpedia.org/Portal:Legislative_Branch "Portal:Legislative Branch") On May 15, 2015, the [House](https://ballotpedia.org/United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives") passed [HR 1735—the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2016](https://www.congress.gov/bill/114th-congress/house-bill/1735?q=%7B%22search%22%3A%5B%22hr+1735%22%5D%7D)—by a vote of 269-151. The second version of the $607 billion national defense bill included $5 billion in cuts to match what was approved in the budget and language preventing the closure of the Guantanamo Bay military prison.[[94]](https://ballotpedia.org/Filemon_Vela_(Texas_U.S._representative)#cite_note-94)[[95]](https://ballotpedia.org/Filemon_Vela_(Texas_U.S._representative)#cite_note-95) Vela voted with 134 other [Democrats](https://ballotpedia.org/Democrats "Democrats") and 235 [Republicans](https://ballotpedia.org/Republicans "Republicans") to approve the bill.[[96]](https://ballotpedia.org/Filemon_Vela_(Texas_U.S._representative)#cite_note-96) On November 10, 2015, the [Senate](https://ballotpedia.org/United_States_Senate "United States Senate") passed the bill by a vote of 91-3, and President [Barack Obama](https://ballotpedia.org/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") signed it into law on November 25, 2015.[[97]](https://ballotpedia.org/Filemon_Vela_(Texas_U.S._representative)#cite_note-97) ##### 2016 Budget proposal [![Image 132: Nay3.png](https://cdn.ballotpedia.org/images/thumb/e/ea/Nay3.png/55px-Nay3.png)](https://ballotpedia.org/Portal:Legislative_Branch "Portal:Legislative Branch") On April 30, 2015, the [House](https://ballotpedia.org/United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives") voted to approve [SConRes11](https://www.congress.gov/bill/114th-congress/senate-concurrent-resolution/11), a congressional budget proposal for fiscal year 2016, by a vote of 226-197. The bill increased military and domestic spending levels and suspended the debt ceiling until March 2017.[[101]](https://ballotpedia.org/Filemon_Vela_(Texas_U.S._representative)#cite_note-101) Vela voted with 186 [Democrats](https://ballotpedia.org/Democrats "Democrats") and 79 [Republicans](https://ballotpedia.org/Republicans "Republicans") in favor of the bill.[[102]](https://ballotpedia.org/Filemon_Vela_(Texas_U.S._representative)#cite_note-102) It passed the [Senate](https://ballotpedia.org/United_States_Senate "United States Senate") on October 30, 2015.[[103]](https://ballotpedia.org/Filemon_Vela_(Texas_U.S._representative)#cite_note-103) President [Barack Obama](https://ballotpedia.org/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") signed it into law on November 2, 2015. #### Foreign Affairs ##### Iran nuclear deal _See also: [Iran nuclear agreement, 2015](https://ballotpedia.org/Iran\_nuclear\_agreement,\_2015 "Iran nuclear agreement, 2015")_ [![Image 134: Yea3.png](https://cdn.ballotpedia.org/images/thumb/c/cd/Yea3.png/50px-Yea3.png)](https://ballotpedia.org/Portal:Legislative_Branch "Portal:Legislative Branch") On May 14, 2015, the [House](https://ballotpedia.org/United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives") approved [HR 1191—the Iran Nuclear Agreement Review Act of 2015](https://www.congress.gov/bill/114th-congress/house-bill/1191/actions)—by a vote of 400-25. The bill required President [Barack Obama](https://ballotpedia.org/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") to submit the details of the nuclear deal with Iran for congressional review. [Congress](https://ballotpedia.org/United_States_Congress "United States Congress") had 60 days to review the deal and vote to approve, disapprove, or take no action on the deal. During the review period, sanctions on Iran could not be lifted. Vela voted with 176 [Democrats](https://ballotpedia.org/Democrats "Democrats") to approve the bill.[[104]](https://ballotpedia.org/Filemon_Vela_(Texas_U.S._representative)#cite_note-104)[[105]](https://ballotpedia.org/Filemon_Vela_(Texas_U.S._representative)#cite_note-105) **Approval of Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action** [![Image 135: Nay3.png](https://cdn.ballotpedia.org/images/thumb/e/ea/Nay3.png/55px-Nay3.png)](https://ballotpedia.org/Portal:Legislative_Branch "Portal:Legislative Branch") On September 11, 2015, the [House](https://ballotpedia.org/United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives") rejected [HR 3461—To approve the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, signed at Vienna on July 14, 2015, relating to the nuclear program of Iran](https://www.congress.gov/bill/114th-congress/house-bill/3461)—by a vote of 162-269. The legislation proposed approving [the nuclear agreement with Iran](https://ballotpedia.org/Iran_nuclear_agreement,_2015 "Iran nuclear agreement, 2015"). Vela voted with 24 [Democrats](https://ballotpedia.org/Democrats "Democrats") and 244 [Republicans](https://ballotpedia.org/Republicans "Republicans") against the bill.[[106]](https://ballotpedia.org/Filemon_Vela_(Texas_U.S._representative)#cite_note-106)[[107]](https://ballotpedia.org/Filemon_Vela_(Texas_U.S._representative)#cite_note-107) **Suspension of Iran sanctions relief** [![Image 136: Nay3.png](https://cdn.ballotpedia.org/images/thumb/e/ea/Nay3.png/55px-Nay3.png)](https://ballotpedia.org/Portal:Legislative_Branch "Portal:Legislative Branch") On September 11, 2015, the [House](https://ballotpedia.org/United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives") approved [HR 3460—To suspend until January 21, 2017, the authority of the President to waive, suspend, reduce, provide relief from, or otherwise limit the application of sanctions pursuant to an agreement related to the nuclear program of Iran](https://www.congress.gov/bill/114th-congress/house-bill/3460?q=%7B%22search%22%3A%5B%22Peter+Roskram%22%5D%7D)—by a vote of 247-186. HR 3460 prohibited "the President, prior to January 21, 2017, from: limiting the application of specified sanctions on Iran or refraining from applying any such sanctions; or removing a foreign person (including entities) listed in Attachments 3 or 4 to Annex II of the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPA) from the list of designated nationals and blocked persons maintained by the Office of Foreign Asset Control of the Department of the Treasury." Vela voted with 185 [Democrats](https://ballotpedia.org/Democrats "Democrats") against the bill.[[108]](https://ballotpedia.org/Filemon_Vela_(Texas_U.S._representative)#cite_note-108)[[109]](https://ballotpedia.org/Filemon_Vela_(Texas_U.S._representative)#cite_note-109) **Presidential non-compliance of section 2** [![Image 137: Nay3.png](https://cdn.ballotpedia.org/images/thumb/e/ea/Nay3.png/55px-Nay3.png)](https://ballotpedia.org/Portal:Legislative_Branch "Portal:Legislative Branch") On September 10, 2015, the [House](https://ballotpedia.org/United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives") passed [H Res 411—Finding that the President has not complied with section 2 of the Iran Nuclear Agreement Review Act of 2015](https://www.congress.gov/bill/114th-congress/house-resolution/411)—by a vote of 245-186. Section 2 of the [Iran Nuclear Agreement Review Act of 2015](https://www.congress.gov/bill/114th-congress/house-bill/1191) required the president to submit all materials related to the nuclear agreement for congressional review. House [Republicans](https://ballotpedia.org/Republicans "Republicans") introduced the resolution because two agreements between the International Atomic Energy Agency and Iran were not submitted to Congress. Vela voted with 185 [Democrats](https://ballotpedia.org/Democrats "Democrats") against the resolution.[[110]](https://ballotpedia.org/Filemon_Vela_(Texas_U.S._representative)#cite_note-110)[[111]](https://ballotpedia.org/Filemon_Vela_(Texas_U.S._representative)#cite_note-rc492-111) ##### Export-Import Bank [![Image 138: Yea3.png](https://cdn.ballotpedia.org/images/thumb/c/cd/Yea3.png/50px-Yea3.png)](https://ballotpedia.org/Portal:Legislative_Branch "Portal:Legislative Branch") On October 27, 2015, the [House](https://ballotpedia.org/United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives") passed [HR 597—the Export-Import Bank Reform and Reauthorization Act of 2015](https://www.congress.gov/bill/114th-congress/house-bill/597?q=%7B%22search%22%3A%5B%22%5C%22hr597%5C%22%22%5D%7D&resultIndex=1)—by a vote of 313-118. The bill proposed reauthorizing the Export-Import Bank and allowing it to resume offering assistance in the form of loans and insurance to foreign companies that wanted to buy U.S. goods.[[112]](https://ballotpedia.org/Filemon_Vela_(Texas_U.S._representative)#cite_note-112) Vela voted with 185 [Democrats](https://ballotpedia.org/Democrats "Democrats") and 127 [Republicans](https://ballotpedia.org/Republicans "Republicans") in favor of the bill.[[113]](https://ballotpedia.org/Filemon_Vela_(Texas_U.S._representative)#cite_note-113) #### Domestic ##### USA FREEDOM Act of 2015 [![Image 139: Yea3.png](https://cdn.ballotpedia.org/images/thumb/c/cd/Yea3.png/50px-Yea3.png)](https://ballotpedia.org/Portal:Legislative_Branch "Portal:Legislative Branch") On May 13, 2015, the [House](https://ballotpedia.org/United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives") passed [HR 2048—the Uniting and Strengthening America by Fulfilling Rights and Ensuring Effective Discipline Over Monitoring Act of 2015 or the USA FREEDOM Act of 2015](https://www.congress.gov/bill/114th-congress/house-bill/2048?q=%7B%22search%22%3A%5B%22USA+FREEDOM+Act%22%5D%7D)—by a vote of 338-88. The legislation revised [HR 3199—the USA PATRIOT Improvement and Reauthorization Act of 2005](https://www.congress.gov/bill/109th-congress/house-bill/3199?q=%7B%22search%22%3A%5B%22Patriot+Act%22%5D%7D)—by ending the bulk collection of metadata under Sec. 215 of the act, requiring increased reporting from the [Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court](https://ballotpedia.org/United_States_Foreign_Intelligence_Surveillance_Court "United States Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court"), and requiring the use of "a specific selection term as the basis for national security letters that request information from wire or electronic communication service providers, financial institutions, or consumer reporting agencies." Vela voted with 141 [Democrats](https://ballotpedia.org/Democrats "Democrats") and 196 [Republicans](https://ballotpedia.org/Republicans "Republicans") to approve the legislation. It became law on June 2, 2015.[[114]](https://ballotpedia.org/Filemon_Vela_(Texas_U.S._representative)#cite_note-114)[[115]](https://ballotpedia.org/Filemon_Vela_(Texas_U.S._representative)#cite_note-115) ##### Pain-Capable Unborn Child Protection Act [![Image 140: Nay3.png](https://cdn.ballotpedia.org/images/thumb/e/ea/Nay3.png/55px-Nay3.png)](https://ballotpedia.org/Portal:Legislative_Branch "Portal:Legislative Branch") On May 13, 2015, the [House](https://ballotpedia.org/United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives") passed [HR 36—the Pain-Capable Unborn Child Protection Act](https://www.congress.gov/bill/114th-congress/house-bill/36?q=%7B%22search%22%3A%5B%22hr+36%22%5D%7D)—by a vote of 242-184. **Filemon Vela** ([Democratic Party](https://ballotpedia.org/Democratic_Party)) was a member of the [U.S. House](https://ballotpedia.org/United_States_House_of_Representatives), representing Texas' 34th Congressional District. He assumed office on January 3, 2013. He left office on April 1, 2022.

Vela ([Democratic Party](https://ballotpedia.org/Democratic_Party)) ran for re-election to the [U.S. House](https://ballotpedia.org/United_States_House_of_Representatives) to represent Texas' 34th Congressional District. He won in the general election on [November 3, 2020](https://ballotpedia.org/Texas%27_34th_Congressional_District_election,_2020).

Vela resigned on April 1, 2022 to accept a position at Akin Gump Strauss Hauer & Feld, a lobbying firm in Washington D.C.[[1]](https://ballotpedia.org/Filemon_Vela_(Texas_U.S._representative)#cite_note-1)

Vela is a member of the House Committee on Homeland Security and the House Committee on Agriculture. He is also co-chair of the Congressional Border Caucus.[[2]](https://ballotpedia.org/Filemon_Vela_(Texas_U.S._representative)#cite_note-2)

Before being elected to Congress, Vela worked as a lawyer.

On March 22, 2021, Vela announced he [would not seek re-election](https://ballotpedia.org/List_of_U.S._Congress_incumbents_who_are_not_running_for_re-election_in_2022 "List of U.S. Congress incumbents who are not running for re-election in 2022") in 2022.[[3]](https://ballotpedia.org/Filemon_Vela_(Texas_U.S._representative)#cite_note-3)

## Biography

Vela was born in Harlingen, Texas. He graduated with a bachelor's degree from Georgetown University and his law degree from University of Texas. He has worked as an attorney since his graduation. He once considered running for Congress in the 1980s but his clients kept his focus until he decided to run in 2011.[[4]](https://ballotpedia.org/Filemon_Vela_(Texas_U.S._representative)#cite_note-nj-4)

## Career

Below is an abbreviated outline of Vela's academic, professional, and political career:[[5]](https://ballotpedia.org/Filemon_Vela_(Texas_U.S._representative)#cite_note-5)

*   2013-2022: U.S. Representative from Texas' 34th Congressional District
*   1988-2012: Practicing lawyer
*   1987: Graduated from the University of Texas, Austin, with a J.D.
*   1985: Graduated from Georgetown University with a B.A.

### Key votes: 117th Congress, 2021-2023

The [117th United States Congress](https://ballotpedia.org/117th_United_States_Congress "117th United States Congress") began on January 3, 2021 and ended on January 3, 2023. At the start of the session, Democrats held the majority in the [U.S. House of Representatives](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._House_of_Representatives "U.S. House of Representatives") (222-213), and the [U.S. Senate](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Senate "U.S. Senate") had a 50-50 makeup. Democrats assumed control of the Senate on January 20, 2021, when President [Joe Biden](https://ballotpedia.org/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden") (D) and Vice President [Kamala Harris](https://ballotpedia.org/Kamala_Harris "Kamala Harris") (D), who acted as a tie-breaking vote in the chamber, assumed office. Comparatively, the [113th Congress](https://ballotpedia.org/113th_Congress "113th Congress") had 7.0 percent of introduced bills enacted into law in the second session.[[81]](https://ballotpedia.org/Filemon_Vela_(Texas_U.S._representative)#cite_note-81)[[82]](https://ballotpedia.org/Filemon_Vela_(Texas_U.S._representative)#cite_note-82) For more information pertaining to Vela's voting record in the 114th Congress, please see the below sections.[[83]](https://ballotpedia.org/Filemon_Vela_(Texas_U.S._representative)#cite_note-83) #### Economic and fiscal ##### Trade Act of 2015 _See also: [The Trans-Pacific Partnership trade deal, 2015](https://ballotpedia.org/The\_Trans-Pacific\_Partnership\_trade\_deal,\_2015 "The Trans-Pacific Partnership trade deal, 2015")_ **Trade adjustment assistance** [![Image 126: Nay3.png](https://cdn.ballotpedia.org/images/thumb/e/ea/Nay3.png/55px-Nay3.png)](https://ballotpedia.org/Portal:Legislative_Branch "Portal:Legislative Branch") On June 12, 2015, the [House](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._House_of_Representatives "U.S. House of Representatives") rejected the [trade adjustment assistance (TAA)](https://ballotpedia.org/Trade_adjustment_assistance "Trade adjustment assistance") measure in [HR 1314—the Trade Act of 2015](https://www.congress.gov/bill/114th-congress/house-bill/1314)—by a vote of 126-302. [Trade adjustment assistance (TAA)](https://ballotpedia.org/Trade_adjustment_assistance "Trade adjustment assistance") is a federal program providing American workers displaced by foreign trade agreements with job training and services. The measure was packaged with [trade promotion authority (TPA)](https://ballotpedia.org/Trade_promotion_authority_(TPA) "Trade promotion authority (TPA)"), also known as fast-track authority. TPA is a legislative procedure that allows Congress to define "U.S. negotiating objectives and spells out a detailed oversight and consultation process for during trade negotiations. Under TPA, Congress retains the authority to review and decide whether any proposed U.S. trade agreement will be implemented," according to the Office of the United States Trade Representative. Vela was one of 144 Democrats to vote against the bill.[[84]](https://ballotpedia.org/Filemon_Vela_(Texas_U.S._representative)#cite_note-84)[[85]](https://ballotpedia.org/Filemon_Vela_(Texas_U.S._representative)#cite_note-85) **Trade promotion authority** [![Image 127: Nay3.png](https://cdn.ballotpedia.org/images/thumb/e/ea/Nay3.png/55px-Nay3.png)](https://ballotpedia.org/Portal:Legislative_Branch "Portal:Legislative Branch") On June 12, 2015, the [House](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._House_of_Representatives "U.S. House of Representatives") passed the [trade promotion authority (TPA)](https://ballotpedia.org/Trade_promotion_authority_(TPA) "Trade promotion authority (TPA)") measure in [HR 1314—the Trade Act of 2015](https://www.congress.gov/bill/114th-congress/house-bill/1314) —by a vote of 219-211. TPA gives the [president](https://ballotpedia.org/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") fast-track authority to negotiate trade agreements sent to [Congress](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Congress "U.S. Congress") without the opportunity for amendment or filibuster. Although the House approved TPA, it was a largely symbolic vote given the measure was part of a package trade bill including [trade adjustment assistance (TAA)](https://ballotpedia.org/Trade_adjustment_assistance "Trade adjustment assistance"), which was rejected earlier the same day. The amendment passed by a vote of 218-208, with all voting members of the House maintaining his or her original position on TPA except for [Ted Yoho](https://ballotpedia.org/Ted_Yoho "Ted Yoho") (R-Fla.). Along with [trade promotion authority (TPA)](https://ballotpedia.org/Trade_promotion_authority_(TPA) "Trade promotion authority (TPA)"), which [Congress](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Congress "U.S. Congress") passed as part of [HR 2146—the Defending Public Safety Employees' Retirement Act](https://www.congress.gov/bill/114th-congress/house-bill/2146)—TAA became law on June 29, 2015. The Speaker of the House is not required to vote in “ordinary legislative proceedings, except when such vote would be decisive.” In practice, this means the Speaker of the House rarely votes and only does so when it is politically useful. “Aye” and “Yea” mean the same thing, and so do “No” and “Nay”. Congress uses different words in different sorts of votes.

Notes: The Speaker’s Vote?

The Speaker of the House is not required to vote in “ordinary legislative proceedings, except when such vote would be decisive.” In practice, this means the Speaker of the House rarely votes and only does so when it is politically useful. When the Speaker declines to vote, he or she is simply omitted from the roll call by the House Clerk. (See [House Rules](http://www.gpo.gov/fdsys/pkg/HMAN-113/pdf/HMAN-113-houserules.pdf), Rule I(7).)

“Aye” or “Yea”?

“Aye” and “Yea” mean the same thing, and so do “No” and “Nay”. Congress uses different words in different sorts of votes.

The U.S. Constitution says that bills should be decided on by the “yeas and nays” (Article I, Section 7). Congress takes this literally and uses “yea” and “nay” when voting on the final passage of bills.

All Senate votes use these words. But the House of Representatives uses “Aye” and “No” in other sorts of votes.

**Freshmen/Sophomores:** Freshmen and sophomores are Members of Congress whose first term (in the same chamber at the end of the 116th Congress) was the 116 th Congress (freshmen) or 115 th (sophomores). Members of Congress who took office within the last few months of a Congress are considered freshmen in the next Congress as well.

**Leadership/Ideology:** The leadership and ideology scores are not displayed for Members of Congress who introduced fewer than 10 bills, or, for ideology, for Members of Congress that have a low leadership score, as there is usually not enough data in these cases to compute reliable leadership and ideology statistics.

**Ranking Members (RkMembs):** The chair of a committee is always selected from the political party that holds the most seats in the chamber, called the “majority party”. The “ranking member” (sometimes “RkMembs”) is the title given to the senior-most member of the committee _not_ in the majority party.

**Freshmen/Sophomores:** Freshmen and sophomores are Members of Congress whose first term (in the same chamber at the end of the 115th Congress) was the 115 th Congress (freshmen) or 114 th (sophomores). Members of Congress who took office within the last few months of a Congress are considered freshmen in the next Congress as well.

## Additional Notes

**Leadership/Ideology:** The leadership and ideology scores are not displayed for Members of Congress who introduced fewer than 10 bills, or, for ideology, for Members of Congress that have a low leadership score, as there is usually not enough data in these cases to compute reliable leadership and ideology statistics.

**Missing Bills:** We exclude bills from some statistics where the sponsor’s original intent is not in the final bill because the bill’s text was replaced in whole with unrelated provisions (i.e. it became a vehicle for passage of unrelated provisions).

**Ranking Members (RkMembs):** The chair of a committee is always selected from the political party that holds the most seats in the chamber, called the “majority party”. The “ranking member” (sometimes “RkMembs”) is the title given to the senior-most member of the committee _not_ in the majority party.

**Freshmen/Sophomores:** Freshmen and sophomores are Members of Congress whose first term (in the same chamber at the end of the 113th Congress) was the 113 th Congress (freshmen) or 112 th (sophomores). Members of Congress who took office within the last few months of a Congress are considered freshmen in the next Congress as well.

## Additional Notes

**Leadership/Ideology:** The leadership and ideology scores are not displayed for Members of Congress who introduced fewer than 10 bills, or, for ideology, for Members of Congress that have a low leadership score, as there is usually not enough data in these cases to compute reliable leadership and ideology statistics.

**Missing Bills:** We exclude bills from some statistics where the sponsor’s original intent is not in the final bill because the bill’s text was replaced in whole with unrelated provisions (i.e. it became a vehicle for passage of unrelated provisions).

**Ranking Members (RkMembs):** The chair of a committee is always selected from the political party that holds the most seats in the chamber, called the “majority party”. The “ranking member” (sometimes “RkMembs”) is the title given to the senior-most member of the committee _not_ in the majority party.

**Freshmen/Sophomores:** Freshmen and sophomores are Members of Congress whose first term (in the same chamber at the end of the 113th Congress) was the 113 th Congress (freshmen) or 112 th (sophomores). Members of Congress who took office within the last few months of a Congress are considered freshmen in the next Congress as well.

# 2016 Report Cards 

 Texas Delegation / Missed Votes

These statistics dissect the legislative records of Members of Congress during the 114 th Congress (Jan. 6, 2015-Jan. 3, 2017), as of Aug. 24, 2017.

A higher or lower number below doesn’t necessarily make a legislator any better or worse, or more or less effective, than other Members of Congress. We present these statistics for you to understand the quantitative aspects of legislating and make your own judgements based on what legislative activities you think are important.

Keep in mind that there are many important aspects of being a legislator besides what can be measured, such as constituent services and performing oversight of the executive branch, which aren’t reflected here.

## Additional Notes

**Leadership/Ideology:** The leadership and ideology scores are not displayed for Members of Congress who introduced fewer than 10 bills, or, for ideology, for Members of Congress that have a low leadership score, as there is usually not enough data in these cases to compute reliable leadership and ideology statistics.

**Missing Bills:** We exclude bills from some statistics where the sponsor’s original intent is not in the final bill because the bill’s text was replaced in whole with unrelated provisions (i.e. it became a vehicle for passage of unrelated provisions).

**Ranking Members (RkMembs):** The chair of a committee is always selected from the political party that holds the most seats in the chamber, called the “majority party”. The “ranking member” (sometimes “RkMembs”) is the title given to the senior-most member of the committee _not_ in the majority party.

**Freshmen/Sophomores:** Freshmen and sophomores are Members of Congress whose first term (in the same chamber at the end of the 114th Congress) was the 114 th Congress (freshmen) or 113 th (sophomores). Members of Congress who took office within the last few months of a Congress are considered freshmen in the next Congress as well.

## Additional Notes

**Leadership/Ideology:** The leadership and ideology scores are not displayed for Members of Congress who introduced fewer than 10 bills, or, for ideology, for Members of Congress that have a low leadership score, as there is usually not enough data in these cases to compute reliable leadership and ideology statistics.

**Missing Bills:** We exclude bills from some statistics where the sponsor’s original intent is not in the final bill because the bill’s text was replaced in whole with unrelated provisions (i.e. it became a vehicle for passage of unrelated provisions).

**Ranking Members (RkMembs):** The chair of a committee is always selected from the political party that holds the most seats in the chamber, called the “majority party”. The “ranking member” (sometimes “RkMembs”) is the title given to the senior-most member of the committee _not_ in the majority party.

**Freshmen/Sophomores:** Freshmen and sophomores are Members of Congress whose first term (in the same chamber at the end of the 114th Congress) was the 114 th Congress (freshmen) or 113 th (sophomores). Members of Congress who took office within the last few months of a Congress are considered freshmen in the next Congress as well.

## Additional Notes

**Leadership/Ideology:** The leadership and ideology scores are not displayed for Members of Congress who introduced fewer than 10 bills, or, for ideology, for Members of Congress that have a low leadership score, as there is usually not enough data in these cases to compute reliable leadership and ideology statistics.

**Missing Bills:** We exclude bills from some statistics where the sponsor’s original intent is not in the final bill because the bill’s text was replaced in whole with unrelated provisions (i.e. it became a vehicle for passage of unrelated provisions).

**Ranking Members (RkMembs):** The chair of a committee is always selected from the political party that holds the most seats in the chamber, called the “majority party”. The “ranking member” (sometimes “RkMembs”) is the title given to the senior-most member of the committee _not_ in the majority party.

**Freshmen/Sophomores:** Freshmen and sophomores are Members of Congress whose first term (in the same chamber at the end of the 114th Congress) was the 114 th Congress (freshmen) or 113 th (sophomores). Members of Congress who took office within the last few months of a Congress are considered freshmen in the next Congress as well.

# 2016 Report Cards 

 All Representatives / Missed Votes

These statistics dissect the legislative records of Members of Congress during the 114 th Congress (Jan. 6, 2015-Jan. 3, 2017), as of Aug. 24, 2017.

A higher or lower number below doesn’t necessarily make a legislator any better or worse, or more or less effective, than other Members of Congress. We present these statistics for you to understand the quantitative aspects of legislating and make your own judgements based on what legislative activities you think are important.

Keep in mind that there are many important aspects of being a legislator besides what can be measured, such as constituent services and performing oversight of the executive branch, which aren’t reflected here.

## Additional Notes

**Leadership/Ideology:** The leadership and ideology scores are not displayed for Members of Congress who introduced fewer than 10 bills, or, for ideology, for Members of Congress that have a low leadership score, as there is usually not enough data in these cases to compute reliable leadership and ideology statistics.

**Missing Bills:** We exclude bills from some statistics where the sponsor’s original intent is not in the final bill because the bill’s text was replaced in whole with unrelated provisions (i.e. it became a vehicle for passage of unrelated provisions).

**Ranking Members (RkMembs):** The chair of a committee is always selected from the political party that holds the most seats in the chamber, called the “majority party”. The “ranking member” (sometimes “RkMembs”) is the title given to the senior-most member of the committee _not_ in the majority party.

**Freshmen/Sophomores:** Freshmen and sophomores are Members of Congress whose first term (in the same chamber at the end of the 114th Congress) was the 114 th Congress (freshmen) or 113 th (sophomores). Members of Congress who took office within the last few months of a Congress are considered freshmen in the next Congress as well.

_[EDITOR’S NOTE: This story has been updated with a comment from Republican congressional candidate Mayra Flores.]_

McALLEN, Texas ([Border Report](https://www.borderreport.com/)) — Texas Democrat U.S. Rep. Filemon Vela Jr., retired Thursday night from Congress early, which will prompt a special election for his heated seat representing the South Texas border.

U.S. Rep. Vicente Gonzalez, a Democrat from Texas who currently represents the neighboring congressional district, is running for Vela’s seat in November. He said on Friday he wished Vela well in his early retirement, which took effect at 11:59 p.m. Thursday night.

[DHS says Title 42 ending on May 23 but removals of ineligible migrants will continue](https://www.borderreport.com/hot-topics/immigration/dhs-says-title-42-ending-on-may-23-but-removals-of-ineligible-migrants-will-continue/?ipid=promo-link-block1)

“I join all South Texans in thanking Congressman Filemon Vela for his service and dedication to our region in Congress. Congressman Vela has been a friend, a mentor, and a staunch advocate for our veterans, our students, small businesses and region as a whole. For the past nine years, Congressman Vela was a fighter. He will be missed, and I wish him luck as he embarks on his next chapter,” Gonzalez said.

Video 1

Video 2

Republican nominee Mayra Flores, who is running for Vela’s seat in November against Gonzalez, was upset about the early retirement during a time of economic and security “crisis” on the South Texas border.

Flores told KVEO Reporter Sydney Hernandez on Friday: “Filemon Vela is abandoning us while we have a crisis on our border and families can’t afford groceries and gas because prices are so high. I will never abandon our community and am looking forward to competing in the special election for Texas’ 34th District. We are going to flip this seat and bring our South Texas values of faith, family and freedom to Washington.”

Vela last week told Border Report that he was stepping down early, but did not specify exactly when.

![Image 6](https://www.borderreport.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/28/2022/04/Filemon-Vela-portrait-082219.jpg?w=900)

U.S. Rep. Filemon Vela Jr., is seen at his offices in Brownsville, Texas, on Aug. 22, 2019. (Sandra Sanchez/Border Report File Photo)

U.S. Rep. Filemon Vela Jr., is seen at his offices in Brownsville, Texas, on Aug. 22, 2019. (Sandra Sanchez/Border Report File Photo)

[South Texas border congressman confirms he is retiring early](https://www.borderreport.com/regions/washington-d-c/south-texas-border-congressman-confirms-he-is-retiring-early/?ipid=promo-link-block2)

Vela has represented congressional District 34 for five terms since 2013. He intends to work a law and lobbying firm in Washington, D.C.

Gonzalez is running for District 34 in the fall but won’t give up his current seat representing District 15, he told Border Report last week.

[South Texas border congressman plans to remain in seat even if special election is called](https://www.borderreport.com/news/elections/south-texas-border-congressman-plans-to-remain-in-seat-even-if-special-election-is-called/?ipid=promo-link-block3)

Gonzalez is switching districts due to redistricting maps drawn by the Republican-led Texas Legislature during a Special Session that moved his McAllen home from District 15 into District 34.

Gonzalez said even if Gov. Greg Abbott calls a special election to fill Vela’s vacant seat, he won’t run for it until the general election in November.
